docs.title: Hyperbolic Optics Documentation
docs.text: A comprehensive Python package for simulating the reflective properties of hyperbolic materials and anisotropic structures using the 4×4 transfer matrix method.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Transfer Matrix Method: Accurate 4×4 transfer matrix implementation for anisotropic media
  • Multiple Scenarios: Support for incident angle sweeps, azimuthal rotations, dispersion analysis, and single-point calculations
  • Materials Library: Pre-configured materials including Quartz, Calcite, Sapphire, and Gallium Oxide
  • Mueller Matrix Analysis: Complete Stokes parameter and polarization analysis capabilities
  • Custom Materials: Define arbitrary materials with custom permittivity and permeability tensors
  • Visualization: Publication-quality plotting functions

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure
from hyperbolic_optics.mueller import Mueller

# Define a simple structure
payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Simple",
        "incidentAngle": 45.0,
        "azimuthal_angle": 0.0,
        "frequency": 1460.0
    },
    "Layers": [
        {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
        {"type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer", "thickness": 0.1},
        {
            "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
            "material": "Calcite",
            "rotationX": 0,
            "rotationY": 90,
            "rotationZ": 0
        }
    ]
}

# Run simulation
structure = Structure()
structure.execute(payload)

# Calculate reflectivities
R_pp = abs(structure.r_pp)**2
R_ss = abs(structure.r_ss)**2

print(f"p-polarized reflectivity: {R_pp:.4f}")
print(f"s-polarized reflectivity: {R_ss:.4f}")

docs.title: bcm
docs.text:
Differentiable planar solver: an eigendecomposition-free cascade in JAX.

The NumPy engine (:mod:hyperbolic_optics.structure) diagonalises each layer's 4×4 Berreman matrix, whose eigenvectors are awkward to differentiate (arbitrary phase, divergent derivative at degeneracies, which every isotropic layer has). Here each layer's scattering matrix is built from matrix products and linear solves only, so jax.grad gives exact derivatives with respect to thicknesses, tensors, orientations, angle and wavelength.

For a thin slice, exp(iΔτ) − I is a short Taylor series; 2ᴺ slices are assembled by N doublings, each a Redheffer star product of the interval with itself (the precise integration method of Zhong & Williams 1994, as in Yang, Song & Cai, arXiv:2608.06185). Intervals are carried as wave amplitudes in a reference medium of permittivity 2kx² + 1, whose waves always propagate and are scaled to unit power, so no doubling meets a singular inverse.

Coefficients are Jones matrices [..., out, in] with 0 = p and 1 = s, on the NumPy engine's sign convention. The half-spaces are isotropic and lossless, except in :func:solve_stack_on_crystal. Inputs broadcast over leading batch dimensions. Reference accuracy needs jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True); without it a warning says so.

Classes:

  • PlanarResult –

    Complex Jones matrices and powers, each [..., out, in] with 0 = p, 1 = s.

  • PlanarSMatrix –

    The full bidirectional scattering matrix of a planar stack.

  • StackFields –

    Fields and power flow through a planar stack, for p and s light from the top.

  • CrystalResult –

    Response of a stack on a semi-infinite anisotropic (or lossy) substrate.

Functions:

  • rotation_matrix –

    Euler rotation Rz(z) · Ry(y) · Rx(x) in radians, [..., 3, 3].

  • rotate_tensor –

    Similarity transform R · tensor · Rᵀ, broadcasting over batch dimensions.

  • system_matrix –

    Berreman matrix Δ with dF/dz̃ = iΔF, F = [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy].

  • solve_stack –

    Reflection and transmission of a planar stack of anisotropic layers.

  • stack_smatrix –

    The bidirectional, power-normalized scattering matrix of a planar stack.

  • cascade –

    Connect upper's bottom port to lower's top port.

  • stack_fields –

    Fields, interface fluxes and layer-resolved absorption of a planar stack.

  • solve_stack_on_crystal –

    A planar stack on a semi-infinite anisotropic, lossy or hyperbolic substrate.

docs.title: PlanarResult
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Complex Jones matrices and powers, each [..., out, in] with 0 = p, 1 = s.

docs.title: PlanarSMatrix
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

The full bidirectional scattering matrix of a planar stack.

Attributes:

  • s (Array) –

    [..., 4, 4] indexed [out, in] over :data:PORTS. top is the incident-side half-space, bottom the exit side; p and s are defined in each half-space's own plane of incidence (x-z). Reference planes are the stack's two outer interfaces.

  • propagating (Array) –

    [..., 4], whether each port's wave propagates (it is evanescent in a half-space whose index is below kx).

Amplitudes are scaled by √kz of their half-space, so between propagating ports |s|² is the fraction of power transferred, and a lossless stack has a unitary s. Reciprocal media (symmetric ε and μ) give s(kx) = D · s(−kx)ᵀ · D with D = diag(−1, 1, −1, 1): reversing a wave reverses its in-plane wavevector, and the p waves' sign convention (they share the sign of Hy) flips on reversal. For an evanescent port the same scaling still applies (with complex kz), so matrices of stacks that share a half-space compose correctly through it -- frustrated total internal reflection included -- but |s|² is not a power there.

docs.title: StackFields
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Fields and power flow through a planar stack, for p and s light from the top.

The last axis of every array is the incident polarization (0 = p, 1 = s), each of unit incident power.

Attributes:

  • R, (T) –

    [..., 2] total reflectance and transmittance (summed over the outgoing polarizations).

  • absorption (Array) –

    [..., L, 2] fraction of the incident power absorbed in each layer.

  • interface_flux (Array) –

    [..., L + 1, 2] normal energy flux S_z at each interface, from the top of the first layer down, over the incident flux: 1 − R at the top and T at the bottom.

  • z_um (Array) –

    [..., L·S] depths of the field samples below the top of the first layer (empty unless samples_per_layer was given).

  • fields (Array) –

    [..., L·S, 6, 2] complex (Ex, Ey, Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz) at those depths, H scaled by the free-space impedance.

docs.title: CrystalResult
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Response of a stack on a semi-infinite anisotropic (or lossy) substrate.

Attributes:

  • r (Array) –

    [..., 2, 2] reflection Jones matrix [out, in] (0 = p, 1 = s), on the same convention as :func:solve_stack.

  • R (Array) –

    |r|².

  • T (Array) –

    [..., 2] total power carried into the substrate, per incident polarization, from the normal Poynting flux just inside it (1 − R − T is absorbed in the layers).

docs.title: rotation_matrix
docs.text:
rotation_matrix(x, y, z)

Euler rotation Rz(z) · Ry(y) · Rx(x) in radians, [..., 3, 3].

The payload API's rotationX/rotationY/rotationZ convention, so a tensor rotated with :func:rotate_tensor matches the one a Crystal Layer would use for the same angles.

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/bcm.py 
def rotation_matrix(x: jax.Array, y: jax.Array, z: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Euler rotation ``Rz(z) · Ry(y) · Rx(x)`` in radians, ``[..., 3, 3]``.

    The payload API's ``rotationX``/``rotationY``/``rotationZ`` convention, so a
    tensor rotated with :func:`rotate_tensor` matches the one a ``Crystal Layer``
    would use for the same angles.
    """
    x, y, z = jnp.broadcast_arrays(*(jnp.asarray(angle, dtype=float) for angle in (x, y, z)))
    zero, one = jnp.zeros_like(x), jnp.ones_like(x)

    def matrix(rows):
        return jnp.stack([jnp.stack(row, axis=-1) for row in rows], axis=-2)

    cx, sx, cy, sy, cz, sz = jnp.cos(x), jnp.sin(x), jnp.cos(y), jnp.sin(y), jnp.cos(z), jnp.sin(z)
    rot_x = matrix([[one, zero, zero], [zero, cx, -sx], [zero, sx, cx]])
    rot_y = matrix([[cy, zero, sy], [zero, one, zero], [-sy, zero, cy]])
    rot_z = matrix([[cz, -sz, zero], [sz, cz, zero], [zero, zero, one]])
    return rot_z @ rot_y @ rot_x

def rotate_tensor(tensor: jax.Array, rotation: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Similarity transform ``R · tensor · Rᵀ``, broadcasting over batch dimensions."""
    return rotation @ tensor @ jnp.swapaxes(rotation, -1, -2)

docs.title: system_matrix
docs.text:
system_matrix(eps, mu, kx)

Berreman matrix Δ with dF/dz̃ = iΔF, F = [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy].

Derived from Maxwell's equations with ∂x → i·kx and ∂y → 0 by eliminating the longitudinal components: Ez = a·F from (εE)_z = −kx·Hy and Hz = b·F from (μH)_z = kx·Ey.

Parameters:

  • eps (Array) –

    Permittivity tensor [..., 3, 3].

  • mu (Array) –

    Permeability tensor [..., 3, 3].

  • kx (Array) –

    Normalised in-plane wavevector [...].

Returns:

  • Array –

    [..., 4, 4].

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/bcm.py 
def system_matrix(eps: jax.Array, mu: jax.Array, kx: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Berreman matrix ``Δ`` with ``dF/dz̃ = iΔF``, ``F = [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy]``.

    Derived from Maxwell's equations with ``∂x → i·kx`` and ``∂y → 0`` by
    eliminating the longitudinal components: ``Ez = a·F`` from
    ``(εE)_z = −kx·Hy`` and ``Hz = b·F`` from ``(μH)_z = kx·Ey``.

    Args:
        eps: Permittivity tensor ``[..., 3, 3]``.
        mu: Permeability tensor ``[..., 3, 3]``.
        kx: Normalised in-plane wavevector ``[...]``.

    Returns:
        ``[..., 4, 4]``.
    """
    batch = jnp.broadcast_shapes(eps.shape[:-2], mu.shape[:-2], jnp.shape(kx))
    eps = jnp.broadcast_to(eps, batch + (3, 3))
    mu = jnp.broadcast_to(mu, batch + (3, 3))
    a, b = _longitudinal(eps, mu, kx)
    kx = jnp.broadcast_to(kx, batch).astype(eps.dtype)[..., None]

    def e(i, j):
        return eps[..., i, j][..., None]

    def m(i, j):
        return mu[..., i, j][..., None]

    unit = jnp.eye(4, dtype=eps.dtype)
    ex, ey, hx, hy = unit[0], unit[1], unit[2], unit[3]

    row_ex = kx * a + m(1, 0) * hx + m(1, 1) * hy + m(1, 2) * b
    row_ey = -(m(0, 0) * hx + m(0, 1) * hy + m(0, 2) * b)
    row_hx = kx * b - (e(1, 0) * ex + e(1, 1) * ey + e(1, 2) * a)
    row_hy = e(0, 0) * ex + e(0, 1) * ey + e(0, 2) * a
    return jnp.stack([row_ex, row_ey, row_hx, row_hy], axis=-2)

solve_stack(
    eps,

Reflection and transmission of a planar stack of anisotropic layers.

Parameters:

  • eps (Array) –

    Layer permittivity tensors in the lab frame, [..., L, 3, 3], ordered from the incident side. L may be zero.

  • thickness_um (Array) –

    Layer thicknesses in µm, [..., L].

  • wavelength_um (Array) –

    Vacuum wavelength in µm, [...]. (From a frequency in cm⁻¹: 1e4 / frequency.)

  • incidence_rad (Array) –

    Angle of incidence in the incident medium, radians.

  • eps_incident (Array) –

    Real, positive permittivity of the incident half-space.

  • eps_exit (Array) –

    Real, positive permittivity of the exit half-space.

  • mu (Array | None, default: None ) –

    Layer permeability tensors [..., L, 3, 3]; identity if omitted.

  • doublings (int, default: DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS ) –

    Doublings per layer (static). See :data:DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS.

Returns:

  • PlanarResult –

    class:PlanarResult with r, t, R, T, each

  • PlanarResult –

    [..., 2, 2] indexed [out, in], 0 = p and 1 = s. Wrap in

  • PlanarResult –

    jax.jit(..., static_argnames="doublings") for repeated calls.

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/bcm.py 
def solve_stack(
    eps: jax.Array,
    thickness_um: jax.Array,
    wavelength_um: jax.Array,
    incidence_rad: jax.Array,
    eps_incident: jax.Array,
    eps_exit: jax.Array,
    mu: jax.Array | None = None,
    doublings: int = DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS,
) -> PlanarResult:
    """Reflection and transmission of a planar stack of anisotropic layers.

    Args:
        eps: Layer permittivity tensors in the lab frame, ``[..., L, 3, 3]``,
            ordered from the incident side. ``L`` may be zero.
        thickness_um: Layer thicknesses in µm, ``[..., L]``.
        wavelength_um: Vacuum wavelength in µm, ``[...]``. (From a frequency in
            cm⁻¹: ``1e4 / frequency``.)
        incidence_rad: Angle of incidence in the incident medium, radians.
        eps_incident: Real, positive permittivity of the incident half-space.
        eps_exit: Real, positive permittivity of the exit half-space.
        mu: Layer permeability tensors ``[..., L, 3, 3]``; identity if omitted.
        doublings: Doublings per layer (static). See :data:`DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS`.

    Returns:
        :class:`PlanarResult` with ``r``, ``t``, ``R``, ``T``, each
        ``[..., 2, 2]`` indexed ``[out, in]``, 0 = p and 1 = s. Wrap in
        ``jax.jit(..., static_argnames="doublings")`` for repeated calls.
    """
    _check_x64()
    kx = jnp.sqrt(jnp.asarray(eps_incident)) * jnp.sin(jnp.asarray(incidence_rad))
    t, _, r, _ = _scattering(
        eps, thickness_um, wavelength_um, kx, eps_incident, eps_exit, mu, doublings
    )
    flux = jnp.real(_kz(eps_exit, kx)) / jnp.real(_kz(eps_incident, kx))
    return PlanarResult(r=r, t=t, R=jnp.abs(r) ** 2, T=jnp.abs(t) ** 2 * flux[..., None, None])

The bidirectional, power-normalized scattering matrix of a planar stack.

Where :func:solve_stack gives the response to light from the incident side, this gives all four ports: light from either side, in either polarization, as needed to connect stacks to one another (for instance in a SAX circuit, :mod:hyperbolic_optics.integrations.sax).

Parameters:

  • eps (Array) –

    Layer permittivity tensors [..., L, 3, 3], from the top down.

  • thickness_um (Array) –

    Layer thicknesses in µm, [..., L].

  • wavelength_um (Array) –

    Vacuum wavelength in µm.

  • kx (Array) –

    In-plane wavevector over k₀ (n·sin θ, conserved through the stack), rather than an angle, so stacks sharing a half-space share it too.

  • eps_top, eps_bottom –

    Real, positive permittivities of the half-spaces.

  • mu (Array | None, default: None ) –

    Layer permeability tensors; identity if omitted.

def stack_smatrix(
    eps: jax.Array,
    thickness_um: jax.Array,
    wavelength_um: jax.Array,
    kx: jax.Array,
    eps_top: jax.Array,
    eps_bottom: jax.Array,
    mu: jax.Array | None = None,
    doublings: int = DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS,
) -> PlanarSMatrix:
    """The bidirectional, power-normalized scattering matrix of a planar stack.

    Where :func:`solve_stack` gives the response to light from the incident
    side, this gives all four ports: light from either side, in either
    polarization, as needed to connect stacks to one another (for instance in a
    SAX circuit, :mod:`hyperbolic_optics.integrations.sax`).

    Args:
        eps: Layer permittivity tensors ``[..., L, 3, 3]``, from the top down.
        thickness_um: Layer thicknesses in µm, ``[..., L]``.
        wavelength_um: Vacuum wavelength in µm.
        kx: In-plane wavevector over k₀ (``n·sin θ``, conserved through the
            stack), rather than an angle, so stacks sharing a half-space share
            it too.
        eps_top, eps_bottom: Real, positive permittivities of the half-spaces.
        mu: Layer permeability tensors; identity if omitted.
        doublings: Doublings per layer (static).

    Returns:
        :class:`PlanarSMatrix` over :data:`PORTS`.
    """
    _check_x64()
    kx = jnp.asarray(kx)
    s00, s01, s10, s11 = _scattering(
        eps, thickness_um, wavelength_um, kx, eps_top, eps_bottom, mu, doublings
    )
    return _normalize_smatrix((s00, s01, s10, s11), kx, eps_top, eps_bottom)

Connect upper's bottom port to lower's top port.

The two must share that half-space (same permittivity, same kx): the result is the stack of both, with the shared medium of zero thickness -- what a SAX circuit computes, without SAX. Evanescent channels in the shared medium are carried, so a gap below total internal reflection tunnels.

def cascade(upper: PlanarSMatrix, lower: PlanarSMatrix) -> PlanarSMatrix:
    """Connect ``upper``'s bottom port to ``lower``'s top port.

    The two must share that half-space (same permittivity, same ``kx``): the
    result is the stack of both, with the shared medium of zero thickness --
    what a SAX circuit computes, without SAX. Evanescent channels in the shared
    medium are carried, so a gap below total internal reflection tunnels.
    """

    def blocks(m):
        s = m.s
        return s[..., :2, :2], s[..., 2:, :2], s[..., :2, 2:], s[..., 2:, 2:]

    a_tt, a_bt, a_tb, a_bb = blocks(upper)  # [out side][in side]: t = top, b = bottom
    b_tt, b_bt, b_tb, b_bb = blocks(lower)
    eye = jnp.eye(2, dtype=a_tt.dtype)
    down = _solve(eye - b_tt @ a_bb, b_tt @ a_bt)  # lower's reflection seen from above
    up = _solve(eye - a_bb @ b_tt, a_bb)
    top_top = a_tt + a_tb @ down
    bottom_top = b_bt @ _solve(eye - a_bb @ b_tt, a_bt)
    top_bottom = a_tb @ _solve(eye - b_tt @ a_bb, b_tb)
    bottom_bottom = b_bb + b_bt @ up @ b_tb
    s = jnp.concatenate(
        [
            jnp.concatenate([top_top, top_bottom], axis=-1),
            jnp.concatenate([bottom_top, bottom_bottom], axis=-1),
        ],
        axis=-2,
    )
    propagating = jnp.concatenate([upper.propagating[..., :2], lower.propagating[..., 2:]], axis=-1)
    return PlanarSMatrix(s=s, propagating=propagating)

The fields at each plane come from the scattering matrices of the stack above and below it, never from transfer matrices, so thick, evanescent and strongly absorbing layers stay stable. Everything is differentiable, including with respect to thicknesses: the samples inside a layer sit at fixed fractions of its thickness.

def stack_fields(
    eps: jax.Array,
    thickness_um: jax.Array,
    wavelength_um: jax.Array,
    incidence_rad: jax.Array,
    eps_incident: jax.Array,
    eps_exit: jax.Array,
    mu: jax.Array | None = None,
    samples_per_layer: int = 0,
    doublings: int = DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS,
) -> StackFields:
    """Fields, interface fluxes and layer-resolved absorption of a planar stack.

    The fields at each plane come from the scattering matrices of the stack
    above and below it, never from transfer matrices, so thick, evanescent and
    strongly absorbing layers stay stable. Everything is differentiable,
    including with respect to thicknesses: the samples inside a layer sit at
    fixed fractions of its thickness.

    Args:
        samples_per_layer: Field samples per layer (static), evenly spaced from
            its top to its bottom, both included. ``0`` skips the depth profile.

    The other arguments are as in :func:`solve_stack`.

    Returns:
        :class:`StackFields`.
    """
    _check_x64()
    eps, mu = _materials(eps, mu)
    thickness_um = jnp.asarray(thickness_um)
    eps_incident, eps_exit = jnp.asarray(eps_incident), jnp.asarray(eps_exit)
    n_layers = eps.shape[-3]
    kx = jnp.sqrt(eps_incident) * jnp.sin(jnp.asarray(incidence_rad))
    k0 = 2 * jnp.pi / jnp.asarray(wavelength_um)
    w_ref = _reference_modes(kx)

    deltas = _deltas(eps, mu, kx, w_ref)
    layers = [_layer(deltas[i], k0 * thickness_um[..., i], doublings) for i in range(n_layers)]
    above = [_interface(_isotropic_modes(eps_incident, kx), w_ref)]
    for layer in layers:
        above.append(_star(above[-1], layer))
    below = [_interface(w_ref, _isotropic_modes(eps_exit, kx))]
    for layer in reversed(layers):
        below.insert(0, _star(layer, below[0]))

    incident_flux = 0.5 * jnp.real(_kz(eps_incident, kx))[..., None]
    planes = [_plane_fields(above[j], below[j], w_ref) for j in range(n_layers + 1)]
    flux = jnp.stack([_poynting_z(f) for f in planes], axis=-2) / incident_flux[..., None, :]
    absorption = flux[..., :-1, :] - flux[..., 1:, :]

    batch = flux.shape[:-2]
    z_um = jnp.zeros(batch + (0,))
    fields = jnp.zeros(batch + (0, 6, 2), dtype=eps.dtype)
    if samples_per_layer and n_layers:
        fractions = jnp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, samples_per_layer)
        tops = jnp.cumsum(thickness_um, axis=-1) - thickness_um
        depths, samples = [], []
        for i in range(n_layers):
            k0d = (k0 * thickness_um[..., i])[..., None]
            delta = deltas[i][..., None, :, :]
            upper = _layer(delta, k0d * fractions, doublings)
            lower = _layer(delta, k0d * (1 - fractions), doublings)

            def expand(blocks):
                return tuple(block[..., None, :, :] for block in blocks)

            tangential = _plane_fields(
                _star(expand(above[i]), upper), _star(lower, expand(below[i + 1])),
                w_ref[..., None, :, :],
            )  # fmt: skip
            a, b = _longitudinal(eps[..., i, :, :], mu[..., i, :, :], kx)
            ez = jnp.einsum("...j,...sjn->...sn", a, tangential)
            hz = jnp.einsum("...j,...sjn->...sn", b, tangential)
            full = jnp.stack(
                [tangential[..., 0, :], tangential[..., 1, :], ez,
                 tangential[..., 2, :], tangential[..., 3, :], hz],
                axis=-2,
            )  # fmt: skip
            samples.append(full)
            depths.append(tops[..., i, None] + thickness_um[..., i, None] * fractions)
        fields = jnp.concatenate(jnp.broadcast_arrays(*samples), axis=-3)
        z_um = jnp.concatenate(jnp.broadcast_arrays(*depths), axis=-1)

    return StackFields(
        R=1.0 - flux[..., 0, :],
        T=flux[..., -1, :],
        absorption=absorption,
        interface_flux=flux,
        z_um=z_um,
        fields=fields,
    )

def solve_stack_on_crystal(
    eps: jax.Array,
    thickness_um: jax.Array,
    wavelength_um: jax.Array,
    incidence_rad: jax.Array,
    eps_incident: jax.Array,
    eps_substrate: jax.Array,
    mu: jax.Array | None = None,
    mu_substrate: jax.Array | None = None,
    doublings: int = DEFAULT_DOUBLINGS,
) -> CrystalResult:
    """A planar stack on a semi-infinite anisotropic, lossy or hyperbolic substrate.

    The NumPy engine's ``Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer``, in the
    differentiable solver: bulk crystals (calcite, sapphire, hBN, SiC,
    α-MoO₃, a LiNbO₃ wafer) as substrates, in any orientation. The waves the
    substrate carries away are found without eigendecomposition, by a matrix
    sign function (see :func:`_substrate_modes`), so reflection is exact and
    differentiable even where the substrate's modes are degenerate.

    The other arguments are as in :func:`solve_stack` (``L`` may be zero: a
    bare crystal).

    Args:
        eps_substrate: The substrate's tensor ``[..., 3, 3]`` in the lab frame
            (rotate it with :func:`rotate_tensor`); lossy is fine.
        mu_substrate: Its permeability; identity if omitted.

    Returns:
        :class:`CrystalResult`: ``r``, ``R`` and the power transmitted into
        the substrate ``T``.
    """
    _check_x64()
    eps_substrate, mu_substrate = _materials(eps_substrate, mu_substrate)
    eps_incident = jnp.asarray(eps_incident)
    kx = jnp.sqrt(eps_incident) * jnp.sin(jnp.asarray(incidence_rad))
    # a lossless substrate gets a relative loss of 1e-8 to decide which waves carry energy
    # in; the subspaces are then refined to the lossless ones, so it costs no accuracy
    w_sub = _substrate_modes(eps_substrate, mu_substrate, kx, 1e-8, 60)
    w_in = _isotropic_modes(eps_incident, kx)
    t, _, r, _ = _cascade(eps, mu, thickness_um, wavelength_um, kx, w_in, w_sub, doublings)
    flux = _poynting_z(w_sub[..., :, :2] @ t)  # into the substrate, per input
    incident = 0.5 * jnp.real(_kz(eps_incident, kx))[..., None]
    return CrystalResult(r=r, R=jnp.abs(r) ** 2, T=flux / incident)

Gaussian beams on planar stacks: Goos–Hänchen and Imbert–Fedorov shifts.

A finite beam is a superposition of plane waves. On a planar stack each keeps its in-plane wavevector q, so the beam's angular spectrum passes through component by component, each with the plane-wave S-matrix of :func:hyperbolic_optics.bcm.stack_smatrix at its own q. :func:reflected_beam rebuilds the reflected field on the interface plane, and :func:beam_shift measures its centroid: the Goos–Hänchen shift along the plane of incidence and the Imbert–Fedorov shift across it, which anisotropic and hyperbolic media make large and asymmetric.

    The reflected beam's field on the reference plane, from its angular spectrum.

  • beam_shift –

    Centroid (Δx, Δy) of |field|²: the Goos–Hänchen and Imbert–Fedorov shifts.

def reflected_beam(
    eps, thickness_um, wavelength_um, angle_rad, eps_top, eps_bottom, waist_um,
    polarization=(1.0, 0.0), mu=None, samples: int = 61, span: float = 5.0, points: int = 129,
    extent: float = 4.0,
):  # fmt: skip
    """The reflected beam's field on the reference plane, from its angular spectrum.

    Args:
        polarization: The incident beam's Jones vector ``(p, s)`` on the central wave.
        points, extent: The real-space grid: ``points`` per side over ``±extent``
            footprint widths.
        eps, thickness_um, mu: The layers, as in :func:`hyperbolic_optics.bcm.stack_smatrix`
            (lab frame; the plane of incidence of the central wave is x-z).
        angle_rad: Angle of incidence of the central wave in the top medium.
        eps_top, eps_bottom: The half-spaces' permittivities.
        waist_um: The beam waist ``w₀``.
        samples, span: The angular-spectrum grid (see :func:`_beam_grid`).

    Returns:
        ``(x, y, field)``: coordinates in µm on the interface plane, ``[P]`` each,
        and the reflected field's p and s amplitudes (in the reflected central
        wave's basis) ``[P, P, 2]``.
    """
    grid = _beam_grid(wavelength_um, waist_um, angle_rad, eps_top, samples, span)
    s = _component_smatrices(eps, thickness_um, wavelength_um, grid, eps_top, eps_bottom, mu)
    c_in = _jones(grid, eps_top, forward=True) @ jnp.asarray(polarization, dtype=complex)
    c_out = _jones(grid, eps_top, forward=False)
    local = s[:, :2, :2] @ c_in[..., None]
    amplitude = (jnp.conj(jnp.swapaxes(c_out, -1, -2)) @ local)[..., 0]  # [K, 2]
    spectrum = jnp.sqrt(grid.weight)[:, None] * amplitude
    k0 = 2 * jnp.pi / jnp.asarray(wavelength_um)
    footprint = jnp.asarray(waist_um) / jnp.cos(angle_rad)
    x = jnp.linspace(-extent, extent, points) * footprint
    y = jnp.linspace(-extent, extent, points) * jnp.asarray(waist_um)
    dqx, dqy = grid.qx - grid.q0[0], grid.qy - grid.q0[1]
    phase = jnp.exp(
        1j * k0 * (dqx[:, None, None] * x[None, :, None] + dqy[:, None, None] * y[None, None, :])
    )
    field = jnp.einsum("kxy,kc->xyc", phase, spectrum)
    return x, y, field

def beam_shift(x, y, field) -> tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array]:
    """Centroid ``(Δx, Δy)`` of ``|field|²``: the Goos–Hänchen and Imbert–Fedorov shifts."""
    intensity = jnp.sum(jnp.abs(field) ** 2, -1)
    total = jnp.sum(intensity)
    return (
        jnp.sum(intensity * x[:, None]) / total,
        jnp.sum(intensity * y[None, :]) / total,
    )

Differentiable permittivity of the built-in materials, in JAX.

The models of :mod:hyperbolic_optics.materials, evaluated in JAX so that wavelength gradients include the dispersion. Parameters come from the same material_params.json; the tests check the two agree.

Models:

  • transparency-window crystals (LiNbO₃, TiO₂, quartz, calcite, sapphire) and PIC materials (SiO₂, Si₃N₄, Si): lossless Sellmeier fits per principal axis;

Crystal-frame permittivity tensor of a built-in material, [..., 3, 3].

Parameters:

  • material (str) –

    A name from :func:materials, e.g. "hBN".

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/dispersion.py 
def permittivity(material: str, wavenumber_cm: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Crystal-frame permittivity tensor of a built-in material, ``[..., 3, 3]``.

    Args:
        material: A name from :func:`materials`, e.g. ``"hBN"``.
        wavenumber_cm: Frequency in cm⁻¹, any shape; differentiable.
    """
    kind, model = _model(material)
    w = jnp.asarray(wavenumber_cm, dtype=float)
    zero = jnp.zeros(w.shape, dtype=complex)
    if kind == "sellmeier":
        lam_sq = (1e4 / w) ** 2

        def sellmeier(axis):
            eps = axis["constant"] + zero
            for a, b in axis["resonances"]:
                eps = eps + a * lam_sq / (lam_sq - b)
            for d, e in axis["poles"]:
                eps = eps + d / (lam_sq - e)
            return eps

        ordinary = sellmeier(model["ordinary"])
        return _diagonal(ordinary, ordinary, sellmeier(model["extraordinary"]))
    if kind == "uniaxial":
        ordinary = _factorised(model["ordinary"], w)
        diagonal = (ordinary, ordinary, _factorised(model["extraordinary"], w))
        return _diagonal(*diagonal)
    if kind == "biaxial":
        return _diagonal(*(_factorised(model[axis], w) for axis in ("x", "y", "z")))
    bu = _lorentz(model["bu"], w)
    alpha = model["bu"]["alpha_tn"] * np.pi / 180.0  # stored complex, as the NumPy model uses it
    xx = model["bu_high"]["xx"] + jnp.sum(bu * np.cos(alpha) ** 2, axis=-1)
    xy = model["bu_high"]["xy"] + jnp.sum(bu * np.sin(alpha) * np.cos(alpha), axis=-1)
    yy = model["bu_high"]["yy"] + jnp.sum(bu * np.sin(alpha) ** 2, axis=-1)
    zz = model["au_high"] + jnp.sum(_lorentz(model["au"], w), axis=-1)
    rows = [[xx, xy, zero], [xy, yy, zero], [zero, zero, zz]]
    return jnp.stack([jnp.stack(row, axis=-1) for row in rows], axis=-2)

In the crystal frame: z the optic © axis, x perpendicular to a mirror plane. In contracted notation r = [[0, −r22, r13], [0, r22, r13], [0, 0, r33], [0, r51, 0], [r51, 0, 0], [−r22, 0, 0]].

def trigonal_3m(r13: float, r22: float, r33: float, r51: float) -> jax.Array:
    """The electro-optic tensor ``rᵢⱼₖ`` ``[3, 3, 3]`` (pm/V) of a point-group-3m crystal.

    In the crystal frame: z the optic (c) axis, x perpendicular to a mirror
    plane. In contracted notation ``r = [[0, −r22, r13], [0, r22, r13],
    [0, 0, r33], [0, r51, 0], [r51, 0, 0], [−r22, 0, 0]]``.
    """
    contracted = jnp.array(
        [[0.0, -r22, r13], [0.0, r22, r13], [0.0, 0.0, r33],
         [0.0, r51, 0.0], [r51, 0.0, 0.0], [-r22, 0.0, 0.0]]
    )  # fmt: skip
    r = jnp.zeros((3, 3, 3))
    for index, (i, j) in enumerate(_VOIGT):
        r = r.at[i, j, :].set(contracted[index])
        r = r.at[j, i, :].set(contracted[index])
    return r

    The electro-optic tensor [3, 3, 3] in the crystal frame (e.g. :data:LITHIUM_NIOBATE).

    The applied field in the lab frame [..., 3], V/µm.

  • rotation (Array | None, default: None ) –

    The crystal's orientation, R with ε_lab = R·ε_crystal·Rᵀ (:func:hyperbolic_optics.bcm.rotation_matrix); identity if omitted.

The Pockels effect: the impermeability η = ε⁻¹ changes by Δηᵢⱼ = Σₖ rᵢⱼₖ Eₖ (1e-6 per pm/V · V/µm).

    ε(E) in the lab frame [..., 3, 3]; differentiable in every argument.

def pockels_tensor(
    eps_crystal: jax.Array,
    r_pm_per_v: jax.Array,
    field_v_per_um: jax.Array,
    rotation: jax.Array | None = None,
) -> jax.Array:
    """The permittivity under an applied field, in the lab frame.

    Args:
        eps_crystal: The unperturbed tensor in the crystal frame ``[..., 3, 3]``
            (e.g. ``dispersion.at_wavelength("LiNbO3", 1.55)``).
        r_pm_per_v: The electro-optic tensor ``[3, 3, 3]`` in the crystal
            frame (e.g. :data:`LITHIUM_NIOBATE`).
        field_v_per_um: The applied field in the lab frame ``[..., 3]``, V/µm.
        rotation: The crystal's orientation, ``R`` with ``ε_lab = R·ε_crystal·Rᵀ``
            (:func:`hyperbolic_optics.bcm.rotation_matrix`); identity if omitted.

    The Pockels effect: the impermeability ``η = ε⁻¹`` changes by
    ``Δηᵢⱼ = Σₖ rᵢⱼₖ Eₖ`` (``1e-6`` per pm/V · V/µm).

    Returns:
        ``ε(E)`` in the lab frame ``[..., 3, 3]``; differentiable in every argument.
    """
    eps_crystal = jnp.asarray(eps_crystal, dtype=complex)
    rotation = jnp.eye(3) if rotation is None else jnp.asarray(rotation)
    field_crystal = jnp.einsum("...ji,...j->...i", rotation, jnp.asarray(field_v_per_um))
    delta_eta = 1e-6 * jnp.einsum("ijk,...k->...ij", jnp.asarray(r_pm_per_v), field_crystal)
    eta = jnp.linalg.inv(eps_crystal) + delta_eta
    return bcm.rotate_tensor(jnp.linalg.inv(eta), rotation)

docs.title: fields
docs.text:
Numerical transmission, layer-resolved absorption, and field profiles.

Where :mod:hyperbolic_optics.structure stops at reflection coefficients, this module reconstructs the field through the stack and derives power quantities from it directly (no closed-form transmission formulas). The tangential field F = [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy] is continuous across interfaces and propagated by the stored layer matrices (Gᵢ = Mᵢ · G_{i+1}); the normal energy flux is S_z = ½ Re(Ex·Hy* − Ey·Hx*). For unit incident power this gives reflectance R = 1 − S_z(G₁)/S_z^inc, transmittance T = S_z(G_exit)/S_z^inc, and layer absorption Aᵢ = [S_z(Gᵢ) − S_z(G_{i+1})]/S_z^inc, which conserve energy exactly (R + T + ΣAᵢ = 1). For a single semi-infinite anisotropic exit there are no interior layers and :meth:FieldProfile.field_profile shows T absorbed with depth (decay length set by Im(kz)).

References:

  • Passler, Jeannin & Paarmann, JOSA B 37, 1060 (2020); arXiv:2002.03832
  • pyGTM: System.calculate_Efield / calculate_Poynting_Absorption_vs_z
  • Passler & Paarmann, JOSA B 34, 2128-2139 (2017)

FieldProfile(structure)

Numerical transmission, layer-resolved absorption, and field profiles.

Consumes an executed :class:~hyperbolic_optics.structure.Structure (mirrors how :class:~hyperbolic_optics.mueller.Mueller consumes one) and exposes the power quantities and field reconstruction described in the module docstring.

The engine is fully batched over the canonical [A, B, F] axes, so :meth:transmittance, :meth:reflectance and :meth:layer_absorption return arrays in the same presentation layout as structure.r_pp. :meth:field_profile adds a depth axis; it broadcasts too, but a full angle/frequency sweep × n_points × 6 field components is multi-gigabyte, so it is intended for the Simple scenario (or a single (angle, frequency) slice).

Examples:

>>> structure = Structure()
>>> structure.execute(payload)
>>> fp = FieldProfile(structure)
>>> fp.transmittance("p")          # power transmittance T
>>> fp.layer_absorption("p")       # per-interior-layer absorption
>>> fp.check_flux_bookkeeping("p")     # max |R + T + ΣA − 1|
>>> prof = fp.field_profile("p")   # dict: z, Ex..Hz, Sz, absorption_*

Note

Works with either backend. Under backend="scattering" the interface fields are recovered from the Redheffer cascade rather than by propagating the per-layer transfer matrices, so the power quantities stay correct for the thick / lossy / evanescent stacks that backend exists for. The two agree to round-off wherever the transfer product is well-conditioned.

def __init__(self, structure: Structure) -> None:
    """Cache the executed structure's transfer matrices and propagation constants.

    Args:
        structure: A :class:`Structure` on which ``execute`` has already run.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the structure has not been executed.

    Note:
        Works with either backend. Under ``backend="scattering"`` the
        interface fields are recovered from the Redheffer cascade rather
        than by propagating the per-layer transfer matrices, so the power
        quantities stay correct for the thick / lossy / evanescent stacks
        that backend exists for. The two agree to round-off wherever the
        transfer product is well-conditioned.
    """
    self.use_cascade = getattr(structure, "backend", None) == "scattering"
    if structure.transfer_matrix is None and not self.use_cascade:
        raise ValueError("Structure has not been executed; call structure.execute(payload).")
    self.structure = structure
    self.layers = structure.layers
    self.n_layers = len(self.layers)
    self.gamma = structure.transfer_matrix  # canonical [A, B, F, 4, 4]
    self.k_x = np.asarray(structure.k_x, dtype=np.complex128)  # [A, 1, 1]
    self.k_0 = np.asarray(structure.k_0, dtype=np.complex128)  # [1, 1, F]
    # Incident dynamical matrix A_inc = inv(prism transfer matrix); maps mode
    # amplitudes -> tangential field in the prism. [A, 1, 1, 4, 4].
    self.a_inc = np.linalg.inv(self.layers[0].matrix)

reflectance(polarization='p')

Total power reflectance R for the given incident polarization.

R = 1 − S_z(G₁)/S_z^inc. For pure p/s incidence this equals |r_pp|²+|r_ps|² / |r_ss|²+|r_sp|² (a useful normalization check). Both coefficients carry the incident polarization second, matching the r_{out,in} convention documented on :meth:transmission_coefficients; the pairing here previously named the other cross term and so disagreed with what this method returns. Returned in the scenario's presentation shape (scalar for Simple).

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/fields.py 
def reflectance(self, polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p") -> np.ndarray:
    """Total power reflectance ``R`` for the given incident polarization.

    ``R = 1 − S_z(G₁)/S_z^inc``. For pure p/s incidence this equals
    ``|r_pp|²+|r_ps|²`` / ``|r_ss|²+|r_sp|²`` (a useful normalization check).
    Both coefficients carry the incident polarization second, matching the
    ``r_{out,in}`` convention documented on
    :meth:`transmission_coefficients`; the pairing here previously named the
    other cross term and so disagreed with what this method returns.
    Returned in the scenario's presentation shape (scalar for ``Simple``).
    """
    _, _, _, s_inc, fields = self._solve(polarization)
    return present(1.0 - _poynting_z(fields[1]) / s_inc)

T = S_z(G_exit)/S_z^inc. For a transparent substrate this is the power that propagates away; for a lossy semi-infinite exit it is the power delivered into (and ultimately absorbed by) the bulk -- see :meth:field_profile for the depth distribution. Presentation shape.

def transmittance(self, polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p") -> np.ndarray:
    """Power transmittance ``T`` -- the flux crossing into the exit medium.

    ``T = S_z(G_exit)/S_z^inc``. For a transparent substrate this is the power
    that propagates away; for a lossy semi-infinite exit it is the power
    delivered into (and ultimately absorbed by) the bulk -- see
    :meth:`field_profile` for the depth distribution. Presentation shape.
    """
    _, _, _, s_inc, fields = self._solve(polarization)
    return present(_poynting_z(fields[-1]) / s_inc)

docs.text:
transmission_coefficients()

Amplitude transmission coefficients t_pp, t_ss, t_ps, t_sp.

These are the field-amplitude analogues of r_pp … -- exactly the coefficients pyGTM exposes from calculate_r_t and the quantities the field reconstruction is built on. They are the (s, p) forward transmission matrix T = M2⁻¹ (M2 = the forward sub-block of Γ), so c_exit = T · [a_s, a_p]. Naming follows the package convention t_{in→out} (matching r_*): e.g. t_ps is the s wave transmitted by incident p. They equal Structure.calculate_transmissivity exactly; transmittance then converts |amplitude|² to power with the correct Poynting/impedance weighting. Presentation shape.

For crystal exits these are eigenmode coordinates. At a degeneracy their basis can rotate between eigensolvers, changing the coefficients; reconstructed fields and power remain invariant.

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/fields.py 
def transmission_coefficients(self) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Amplitude transmission coefficients ``t_pp, t_ss, t_ps, t_sp``.

    These are the field-amplitude analogues of ``r_pp …`` -- exactly the
    coefficients pyGTM exposes from ``calculate_r_t`` and the quantities the
    field reconstruction is built on. They are the ``(s, p)`` forward
    transmission matrix ``T = M2⁻¹`` (``M2`` = the forward sub-block of ``Γ``),
    so ``c_exit = T · [a_s, a_p]``. Naming follows the package convention
    ``t_{in→out}`` (matching ``r_*``): e.g. ``t_ps`` is the s wave transmitted
    by incident p. They equal ``Structure.calculate_transmissivity`` exactly;
    ``transmittance`` then converts |amplitude|² to *power* with the correct
    Poynting/impedance weighting. Presentation shape.

    For crystal exits these are eigenmode coordinates. At a degeneracy
    their basis can rotate between eigensolvers, changing the coefficients;
    reconstructed fields and power remain invariant.
    """
    if self.use_cascade:
        stable = scattering_coefficients(self.layers, self.k_0)
        return {name: present(stable[name]) for name in ("t_ss", "t_ps", "t_sp", "t_pp")}

    g = self.gamma
    row0 = np.stack([g[..., _S_FWD, _S_FWD], g[..., _S_FWD, _P_FWD]], axis=-1)
    row1 = np.stack([g[..., _P_FWD, _S_FWD], g[..., _P_FWD, _P_FWD]], axis=-1)
    m2 = np.stack([row0, row1], axis=-2)  # [A, B, F, 2, 2]; rows/cols = (s, p)
    t = np.linalg.inv(m2)  # T[out, in]: row = transmitted (s, p), col = incident (s, p)
    return {
        "t_ss": present(t[..., 0, 0]),
        "t_ps": present(t[..., 0, 1]),  # in p -> out s
        "t_sp": present(t[..., 1, 0]),  # in s -> out p
        "t_pp": present(t[..., 1, 1]),
    }

def layer_absorption(
    self, polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p"
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Layer-resolved absorptance for each finite interior layer.

    Returns:
        A list (top→bottom) of dicts ``{"index", "type", "absorptance"}``, where
        ``absorptance`` is the fraction of incident power dissipated in that
        layer, in presentation shape. Empty for a prism + semi-infinite-exit

    return [
        {"index": i, "type": layer_type, "absorptance": present(absorbed)}
        for i, layer_type, absorbed in self._layer_absorption_canonical(s_inc, fields)
    ]

docs.text:
summary(polarization='p')

One-call R, T, per-layer absorption, total, and conservation residual.

flux_bookkeeping_residual = max|R + T + ΣAᵢ − 1| over the batch.

Warning

This is a bookkeeping check, not a physics check. The per-layer absorptances are defined as successive differences of the same interface fluxes that R and T are built from, so the sum telescopes and the residual is algebraically zero however wrong the fields are -- it returns machine epsilon even where R exceeds 1. Use it to catch NaN propagation. For an assertion that can fail on bad physics, check passivity instead: every layer absorptance and T non-negative, and R at most 1.

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/fields.py 
def summary(self, polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p") -> dict[str, Any]:
    """One-call ``R``, ``T``, per-layer absorption, total, and conservation residual.

    ``flux_bookkeeping_residual = max|R + T + ΣAᵢ − 1|`` over the batch.

    Warning:
        This is a bookkeeping check, not a physics check. The per-layer
        absorptances are defined as successive differences of the same
        interface fluxes that ``R`` and ``T`` are built from, so the sum
        telescopes and the residual is algebraically zero however wrong the
        fields are -- it returns machine epsilon even where ``R`` exceeds 1.
        Use it to catch NaN propagation. For an assertion that can fail on
        bad physics, check passivity instead: every layer absorptance and
        ``T`` non-negative, and ``R`` at most 1.
    """
    _, _, _, s_inc, fields = self._solve(polarization)
    r = 1.0 - _poynting_z(fields[1]) / s_inc
    t = _poynting_z(fields[-1]) / s_inc
    per_layer = self._layer_absorption_canonical(s_inc, fields)
    total_abs = sum((a for _, _, a in per_layer), start=np.zeros_like(r))
    residual = np.abs(r + t + total_abs - 1.0)
    return {
        "R": present(r),
        "T": present(t),
        "layers": [
            {"index": i, "type": ty, "absorptance": present(a)} for i, ty, a in per_layer
        ],
        "total_absorption": present(total_abs),
        "flux_bookkeeping_residual": float(np.max(residual)),
    }

polarization_resolved(polarization='p')

Experimental. Split R and T into co- and cross-polarized channels.

For a pure "p" or "s" incidence, the reflected/transmitted power is decomposed into the co-polarized channel (same polarization as incident) and the cross-polarized channel (the polarization-converted light — the power analogue of r_ps / t_ps). The conversion fractions cross / (co + cross) quantify how much light changed polarization.

Reflection is split exactly (R_co = |r_co|², R_cross = |r_cross|², reflection being back into the same prism). Transmission is split via the per-mode flux of the two forward exit waves.

Experimental / caveat: the transmitted s/p split is rigorous only for an isotropic exit medium, where the two exit eigenmodes are clean s and p and their fluxes add (T_co + T_cross = T). For an anisotropic exit the eigenmodes are elliptical, so the split is an eigenmode-resolved approximation and may not sum exactly to the total transmittance.

Parameters:

  • polarization (str, default: 'p' ) –

    "p" or "s" (co/cross is undefined for a mixed Jones state).

Returns:

  • dict[str, ndarray] –

    Dict (presentation shape) with R_co, R_cross, T_co, T_cross and

  • dict[str, ndarray] –

    conversion_reflection, conversion_transmission.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If polarization is not "p" or "s".

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/fields.py 
def polarization_resolved(self, polarization: str = "p") -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """**Experimental.** Split R and T into co- and cross-polarized channels.

    For a pure ``"p"`` or ``"s"`` incidence, the reflected/transmitted power is
    decomposed into the *co-polarized* channel (same polarization as incident)
    and the *cross-polarized* channel (the polarization-converted light — the
    power analogue of ``r_ps`` / ``t_ps``). The conversion fractions
    ``cross / (co + cross)`` quantify how much light changed polarization.

    Reflection is split exactly (``R_co = |r_co|²``, ``R_cross = |r_cross|²``,
    reflection being back into the same prism). Transmission is split via the
    per-mode flux of the two forward exit waves.

    Experimental / caveat: the transmitted s/p split is rigorous only for an
    **isotropic exit** medium, where the two exit eigenmodes are clean s and p
    and their fluxes add (``T_co + T_cross = T``). For an anisotropic exit the
    eigenmodes are elliptical, so the split is an eigenmode-resolved
    approximation and may not sum exactly to the total transmittance.

    Args:
        polarization: ``"p"`` or ``"s"`` (co/cross is undefined for a mixed
            Jones state).

    Returns:
        Dict (presentation shape) with ``R_co, R_cross, T_co, T_cross`` and
        ``conversion_reflection``, ``conversion_transmission``.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``polarization`` is not ``"p"`` or ``"s"``.
    """
    key = polarization.lower() if isinstance(polarization, str) else None
    if key not in ("p", "s"):
        raise ValueError("polarization_resolved requires pure 'p' or 's' incidence.")
    _, _, c_exit, s_inc, _ = self._solve(polarization)

    # Reflected amplitudes are the backward slots of c_inc = Gamma @ c_exit.
    c_inc = _matvec(self.gamma, c_exit)
    refl_s, refl_p = c_inc[..., _S_BWD], c_inc[..., _P_BWD]

    # Per-mode transmitted flux (exit modes: index 0 = s-like, 1 = p-like).
    w_full, _, amps = self._exit_transmitted_modes(c_exit)
    tangential = w_full[..., [0, 1, 3, 4], :]  # [..., (Ex,Ey,Hx,Hy), 2]

    def mode_transmittance(mode: int) -> np.ndarray:
        field = amps[..., mode][..., np.newaxis] * tangential[..., :, mode]
        return _poynting_z(field) / s_inc

    t_s, t_p = mode_transmittance(0), mode_transmittance(1)

    if key == "p":
        r_co, r_cross, t_co, t_cross = refl_p, refl_s, t_p, t_s
    else:
        r_co, r_cross, t_co, t_cross = refl_s, refl_p, t_s, t_p

    r_co_pow = np.abs(r_co) ** 2
    r_cross_pow = np.abs(r_cross) ** 2

    def _fraction(cross: np.ndarray, co: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        total = co + cross
        return np.where(np.abs(total) > 1e-30, cross / total, 0.0)

    return {
        "R_co": present(r_co_pow),
        "R_cross": present(r_cross_pow),
        "T_co": present(t_co),
        "T_cross": present(t_cross),
        "conversion_reflection": present(_fraction(r_cross_pow, r_co_pow)),
        "conversion_transmission": present(_fraction(t_cross, t_co)),
    }

def field_profile(
    self,
    polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p",
    n_points: int = 200,
    semi_inf_thickness: float | None = None,
) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Reconstruct ``E(z), H(z)`` and ``S_z(z)`` through the whole stack.

    Args:
        polarization: ``"p"``, ``"s"`` or a complex ``(a_s, a_p)`` Jones pair.
        n_points: Depth samples per layer (interior layers and the exit window).
        semi_inf_thickness: Display window for the semi-infinite exit, in **µm**.
            ``None`` auto-selects ~5 decay lengths of the slowest transmitted
            mode (a few wavelengths if lossless).

    Returns:
        Dict with ``z`` (µm, measured from the first interface) and the squeezed
        field arrays ``Ex, Ey, Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz`` (complex) plus ``Sz`` (real,
        normalized to incident flux). Also ``absorption_cumulative`` =
        ``(Sz[0] − Sz)/1`` running from the surface and ``layer_boundaries`` (µm).

    Note:
        Intended for ``Simple`` / single-point use (the depth axis multiplies
        the batch size); see the class docstring.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a layer thickness is being swept (canonical ``T`` axis
            size > 1) — the depth grid of the swept layer would itself change
            along ``T``, so a field-vs-depth profile is not well defined.
    """
    if self.use_cascade:
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "field_profile requires backend='transfer'. The power quantities "
            "(transmittance, reflectance, layer_absorption, summary) work "
            "under either backend, but resolving the field *with depth* "
            "needs each layer's mode amplitudes at arbitrary z, which the "
            "cascade does not yet expose."
        )
    if self.gamma.shape[T] > 1:
        raise ValueError(
            "field_profile is undefined while sweeping a layer thickness "
            f"(T={self.gamma.shape[T]}); the depth grid changes along T. Profile a "
            "single thickness, or use the power quantities (reflectance/"
            "transmittance/layer_absorption), which support the T axis."
        )
    _, _, c_exit, s_inc, fields = self._solve(polarization)
    cm_to_um = 1.0e4

    z_segments: list[np.ndarray] = []
    comp_segments: list[np.ndarray] = []  # each [..., Nz, 6]
    boundaries = [0.0]
    z_offset = 0.0  # cm

    # Interior finite layers: amplitudes from V^{-1} G_i over all four modes.
    for i in range(1, self.n_layers - 1):
        layer = self.layers[i]
        # T == 1 here (guarded above), so a swept layer's [1,1,1,1] thickness
        # still reduces to a single scalar depth.
        thickness = float(np.asarray(layer.thickness).reshape(-1)[0])
        v_tan, kz = layer.profile.tangential_modes()
        w_full, _ = layer.profile.full_modes()
        amps = np.linalg.solve(v_tan, fields[i][..., np.newaxis])[..., 0]  # [..., 4]
        depth = np.linspace(0.0, thickness, n_points)
        comp_segments.append(self._reconstruct(w_full, kz, amps, depth))
        z_segments.append((z_offset + depth) * cm_to_um)
        z_offset += thickness
        boundaries.append(z_offset * cm_to_um)

    # Semi-infinite exit: two transmitted modes over a display window.
    w_full, kz_exit, amps = self._exit_transmitted_modes(c_exit)
    if semi_inf_thickness is None:
        exit_len = self._auto_semi_infinite_thickness(kz_exit)
    else:
        exit_len = float(semi_inf_thickness) / cm_to_um
    depth = np.linspace(0.0, exit_len, n_points)
    comp_segments.append(self._reconstruct(w_full, kz_exit, amps, depth))
    z_segments.append((z_offset + depth) * cm_to_um)
    boundaries.append((z_offset + exit_len) * cm_to_um)

    components = np.concatenate(comp_segments, axis=-2)  # [..., Nz_total, 6]
    z = np.concatenate(z_segments, axis=-1)
    sz = _poynting_z(components[..., [0, 1, 3, 4]]) / s_inc[..., np.newaxis]

    labels = ("Ex", "Ey", "Ez", "Hx", "Hy", "Hz")
    result: dict[str, np.ndarray] = {"z": z, "layer_boundaries": np.asarray(boundaries)}
    for j, label in enumerate(labels):
        result[label] = np.squeeze(components[..., j])
    sz_sq = np.squeeze(sz)
    result["Sz"] = sz_sq
    result["absorption_cumulative"] = np.take(sz_sq, 0, axis=-1)[..., np.newaxis] - sz_sq
    return result

    S0 (intensity) and S1, S2, S3, and the ellipse parameters

  • dict[str, ndarray] –

    azimuth (ψ, rad) and ellipticity (χ, rad). A single coherent

  • dict[str, ndarray] –

    field is fully polarized, so the degree of polarization is 1 by

  • dict[str, ndarray] –

def stokes_from_field_profile(
    self,
    polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p",
    n_points: int = 200,
    semi_inf_thickness: float | None = None,
) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Polarization state of the transverse field vs depth (Stokes + ellipse).

    Reconstructs the field with :meth:`field_profile` and forms the Stokes
    parameters of the transverse pair ``(Ex, Ey)`` at every depth, so you can
    watch the polarization ellipse evolve as the wave crosses a birefringent
    layer. ``Ex`` is the in-plane (p-like) component, ``Ey`` the out-of-plane
    (s-like) one; the convention is ``e^{-iωt}``.

    Args:
        polarization: ``"p"``, ``"s"`` or a complex ``(a_s, a_p)`` Jones pair.
        n_points: Depth samples per layer (passed to :meth:`field_profile`).
        semi_inf_thickness: Semi-infinite exit display window in µm (see
            :meth:`field_profile`).

    Returns:
        Dict with ``z`` (µm) and ``layer_boundaries`` plus the Stokes profiles
        ``S0`` (intensity) and ``S1, S2, S3``, and the ellipse parameters
        ``azimuth`` (ψ, rad) and ``ellipticity`` (χ, rad). A single coherent
        field is fully polarized, so the degree of polarization is 1 by
        construction and is not returned.

    Note:
        Like :meth:`field_profile`, this is undefined while sweeping a layer
        thickness (raises if the canonical ``T`` axis size > 1).
    """
    profile = self.field_profile(polarization, n_points, semi_inf_thickness)
    ex, ey = profile["Ex"], profile["Ey"]
    ex_sq, ey_sq = np.abs(ex) ** 2, np.abs(ey) ** 2
    s0 = ex_sq + ey_sq
    s1 = ex_sq - ey_sq
    s2 = 2.0 * np.real(ex * np.conj(ey))
    s3 = -2.0 * np.imag(ex * np.conj(ey))
    return {
        "z": profile["z"],
        "layer_boundaries": profile["layer_boundaries"],
        "S0": s0,
        "S1": s1,
        "S2": s2,
        "S3": s3,
        "azimuth": 0.5 * np.arctan2(s2, s1),
        "ellipticity": 0.5 * np.arctan2(s3, np.sqrt(s1**2 + s2**2)),
    }

def tensors(self, wavelength_um: Any) -> tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array | None]:
    """Lab-frame ``(material, background)`` tensors; ``background`` is None if uniform."""
    eps = material_tensor(self.material, wavelength_um, self.rotation_deg)

def half_space_permittivity(self, which: str, wavelength_um: Any) -> jax.Array:
    """Real scalar ε; invalid half-spaces raise eagerly and return NaN under JIT."""
    spec = self.incident if which == "incident" else self.exit
    tensor = material_tensor(spec, jnp.asarray(wavelength_um, dtype=float))
    eps = tensor[..., 0, 0]
    if isinstance(tensor, jax.core.Tracer):
        return jnp.where(_real_scalar(tensor, jnp), eps.real, jnp.nan)
    if not np.all(_real_scalar(tensor, np)):
        raise ValueError(
            f"The {which} half-space ({spec!r}) must be isotropic and lossless; the solvers "
            "need real, positive ε there. Put an absorbing or anisotropic material in a "
            "finite layer instead."
        )
    return eps.real

def exit_medium(self, wavelength_um: Any) -> jax.Array:
    """The exit half-space for 2D-periodic solves (:mod:`~hyperbolic_optics.rcwa2d`).

    A real scalar ε where it is isotropic and lossless; otherwise its 3×3
    tensor -- a crystal, hyperbolic or absorbing substrate, whose two
    transmitted modes then replace p and s. Decided at ``wavelength_um``, or
    under ``jit`` at a representative wavelength of the material.
    """
    wavelength = jnp.asarray(wavelength_um, dtype=float)
    traced = isinstance(wavelength, jax.core.Tracer)
    spec = self.exit
    while isinstance(spec, Oriented):
        spec = spec.material
    if not traced:
        probe = wavelength
    elif isinstance(spec, str):
        probe = 2e4 / sum(dispersion.frequency_range(spec))  # mid-window, cm⁻¹ → µm
    else:
        probe = 1.55
    with jax.ensure_compile_time_eval():  # a static decision, even under jit
        tensor = np.asarray(material_tensor(self.exit, probe))
    if np.all(_real_scalar(tensor, np)):
        return (
            self.half_space_permittivity("exit", wavelength)
            if traced
            else tensor[..., 0, 0].real
        )
    return material_tensor(self.exit, wavelength)

def extract_line_grating(
    component: gf.Component,
    layer: gf.typings.LayerSpec,
    tolerance_um: float | None = None,
) -> LineGrating:
    """Read a line grating back from the polygons of ``component`` on ``layer``.

    Every polygon must be an axis-aligned rectangle; all must span the same y
    range, have the same width, and start at equally spaced x. Anything else
    raises ``ValueError`` naming what failed, because a solver fed a guessed
    geometry returns a confident, wrong answer.

    Args:
        component: A gdsfactory component, e.g. from ``gf.import_gds``.
        layer: The layer the ridges are drawn on.
        tolerance_um: Allowed deviation; defaults to one database unit.

    Returns:
        The :class:`LineGrating`, with the period from a least-squares fit to the
        ridge positions.
    """
    tolerance = component.kcl.dbu * 1.01 if tolerance_um is None else tolerance_um
    layer_index = gf.get_layer(layer)
    polygons = component.get_polygons_points(layers=[layer])
    points = polygons.get(layer_index, [])
    if len(points) < 2:
        raise ValueError(f"need at least two ridges on layer {layer}, found {len(points)}")

    rectangles = []
    for polygon in points:
        polygon = np.asarray(polygon, dtype=float)
        xs, ys = np.unique(np.round(polygon[:, 0], 9)), np.unique(np.round(polygon[:, 1], 9))
        if len(polygon) != 4 or len(xs) != 2 or len(ys) != 2:
            raise ValueError(
                f"polygon on layer {layer} is not an axis-aligned rectangle: {polygon}"
            )
        rectangles.append((xs[0], xs[1], ys[0], ys[1]))
    rectangles.sort()
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = (np.array(column) for column in zip(*rectangles, strict=True))

    if np.ptp(y0) > tolerance or np.ptp(y1) > tolerance:
        raise ValueError("ridges do not all span the same y range; not a line grating")
    widths = x1 - x0
    if np.ptp(widths) > tolerance:
        raise ValueError(f"ridge widths differ by {np.ptp(widths):.4g} µm; not a line grating")
    index = np.arange(len(x0))
    period, start = np.polyfit(index, x0, 1)
    if np.max(np.abs(x0 - (start + period * index))) > tolerance:
        raise ValueError("ridges are not equally spaced; not a periodic line grating")
    if np.mean(widths) >= period - tolerance:  # the fitted period carries rounding
        raise ValueError("ridges touch or overlap; no gap to form a grating")
    return LineGrating(
        period_um=float(period),
        fill=float(np.mean(widths) / period),
        offset=float((start / period) % 1.0),
        n_periods=len(x0),
        length_um=float(np.mean(y1 - y0)),
        origin_um=(float(x0[0]), float(np.mean(y0))),
    )

@gf.cell
def line_grating(
    period_um: float = 2.0,
    fill: float = 0.5,
    n_periods: int = 20,
    length_um: float = 20.0,
    layer: gf.typings.LayerSpec = (1, 0),
) -> gf.Component:
    """PCell: ``n_periods`` ridges of width ``fill · period_um`` and length ``length_um``.

    The period and the ridge width are snapped to the layout grid (the active
    PDK's database unit), so every period drawn is identical; the snapped values
    are recorded in ``component.info`` and are what :func:`extract_line_grating`
    recovers.
    """
    if not 0.0 < fill < 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"fill must lie strictly between 0 and 1, got {fill}")
    component = gf.Component()
    dbu = component.kcl.dbu
    period_dbu = round(period_um / dbu)
    width_dbu = round(fill * period_um / dbu)
    length_dbu = round(length_um / dbu)
    if not 0 < width_dbu < period_dbu:
        raise ValueError("ridge width rounds to zero or to the full period on this grid")
    for index in range(n_periods):
        x0, x1 = index * period_dbu * dbu, (index * period_dbu + width_dbu) * dbu
        top = length_dbu * dbu
        component.add_polygon([(x0, 0.0), (x1, 0.0), (x1, top), (x0, top)], layer=layer)
    component.info["period_um"] = period_dbu * dbu
    component.info["fill"] = width_dbu / period_dbu
    component.info["n_periods"] = n_periods
    component.info["length_um"] = length_dbu * dbu
    return component

def crossed_grating_layers(
    cell: UnitCell | None,
    stack: VerticalStack | Sequence[StackLayer],
    wavelength_um: Any,
) -> list[rcwa2d.PatternedLayer]:
    """:mod:`~hyperbolic_optics.rcwa2d` layers for a unit cell etched into a stack.

    A patterned layer uses its own ``polygons`` if it has them, else the
    cell's shapes (a single etch); ``cell`` may be ``None`` when every
    patterned layer has its own. Polygons, thicknesses, orientations and the
    wavelength may be JAX values.
    """
    layers = stack.layers if isinstance(stack, VerticalStack) else stack
    out = []
    for spec in layers:
        eps, background = spec.tensors(wavelength_um)
        if background is None:
            out.append(rcwa2d.uniform(eps, spec.thickness_um))
        else:
            polygons = spec.polygons if spec.polygons is not None else cell.polygons
            shapes = tuple(rcwa2d.Shape(jnp.asarray(p), eps) for p in polygons)
            out.append(rcwa2d.PatternedLayer(spec.thickness_um, background, shapes))
    return out

A 2D-periodic pattern and the patterned stack its etch makes in the PDK's LayerStack.

The stack is sampled at points inside every shape and around them, in the first cell and in one in the middle of the array; every inside sample must agree, and every outside one, or another layer is patterned differently and a ValueError says so. Where the two columns differ, the layer is patterned (one etch shared by every patterned layer).

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/integrations/gdsfactory/lattice.py 
def crossed_grating_stack(
    component: gf.Component,
    pattern_layer: gf.typings.LayerSpec,
    layer_stack: LayerStack,
    materials: Mapping[str, MaterialSpec] | None = None,
    ambient: MaterialSpec = 1.0,
    period_um: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    samples: int = 3,
    lattice_um: tuple[tuple[float, float], tuple[float, float]] | None = None,
) -> tuple[UnitCell, VerticalStack]:
    """A 2D-periodic pattern and the patterned stack its etch makes in the PDK's LayerStack.

    The stack is sampled at points inside every shape and around them, in the
    first cell and in one in the middle of the array; every inside sample must
    agree, and every outside one, or another layer is patterned differently and
    a ``ValueError`` says so. Where the two columns differ, the layer is
    patterned (one etch shared by every patterned layer).
    """
    cell = extract_unit_cell(component, pattern_layer, period_um, lattice_um)
    a1, a2 = cell._vectors()
    origin = np.asarray(cell.origin_um)
    sites = sorted({(0, 0), (cell.n_cells[0] // 2, cell.n_cells[1] // 2)})
    inside, outside = _sample_points(cell, samples)

    def column(points, where):
        profiles = {
            tuple(vertical_profile(component, layer_stack, tuple(origin + i * a1 + j * a2 + p)))
            for i, j in sites
            for p in points
        }
        if len(profiles) != 1:
            raise ValueError(
                f"The stack varies {where} the shapes on {pattern_layer}: another layer is "
                "patterned differently there, so this is not a single 2D grating in this "
                "layer stack."
            )
        return list(profiles.pop())

    stack = patterned_stack(column(inside, "inside"), column(outside, "around"), materials, ambient)
    return cell, stack

extract_unit_cell(
    component, layer, period_um=None, lattice_um=None
)

Read a 2D-periodic pattern back from the polygons of component on layer.

The polygons are grouped into translated copies of one another. Each group must fill the same complete n₁ × n₂ lattice, so every cell holds the same motif. Shapes must not overlap, even across cell edges, and must not have holes. Anything else raises ValueError, because a solver fed a guessed geometry returns a confident, wrong answer.

Parameters:

  • component (Component) –

    A gdsfactory component, e.g. from gf.import_gds.

  • layer (LayerSpec) –

    The layer the pattern is drawn on.

  • period_um (tuple[float, float] | None, default: None ) –

    A rectangular lattice's period.

  • lattice_um (tuple[tuple[float, float], tuple[float, float]] | None, default: None ) –

    Any lattice's primitive vectors ((a1x, a1y), (a2x, a2y)). Without either, the lattice is inferred -- rectangular, hexagonal or oblique, motifs that repeat a shape (a dimer) included: the shortest basis under which the drawing is one motif on a complete parallelogram of cells. Pass it to impose a lattice instead.

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/integrations/gdsfactory/lattice.py 
def extract_unit_cell(
    component: gf.Component,
    layer: gf.typings.LayerSpec,
    period_um: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    lattice_um: tuple[tuple[float, float], tuple[float, float]] | None = None,
) -> UnitCell:
    """Read a 2D-periodic pattern back from the polygons of ``component`` on ``layer``.

    The polygons are grouped into translated copies of one another. Each group
    must fill the same complete ``n₁ × n₂`` lattice, so every cell holds the
    same motif. Shapes must not overlap, even across cell edges, and must not
    have holes. Anything else raises ``ValueError``, because a solver fed a
    guessed geometry returns a confident, wrong answer.

    Args:
        component: A gdsfactory component, e.g. from ``gf.import_gds``.
        layer: The layer the pattern is drawn on.
        period_um: A rectangular lattice's period.
        lattice_um: Any lattice's primitive vectors ``((a1x, a1y), (a2x, a2y))``.
            Without either, the lattice is inferred -- rectangular, hexagonal or
            oblique, motifs that repeat a shape (a dimer) included: the
            shortest basis under which the drawing is one motif on a complete
            parallelogram of cells. Pass it to impose a lattice instead.
    """
    dbu = component.kcl.dbu
    polygons = _hulls(kf.kdb.Region(component.begin_shapes_rec(gf.get_layer(layer))))
    if len(polygons) < 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"need a repeated pattern on layer {layer}, found {len(polygons)} polygons"
        )

    groups: dict[tuple, list[np.ndarray]] = {}
    for points in polygons:
        groups.setdefault(_shape_key(points), []).append(points)
    corners = {key: np.array([p.min(axis=0) for p in members]) for key, members in groups.items()}

    if lattice_um is None and period_um is not None:
        lattice_um = ((period_um[0], 0.0), (0.0, period_um[1]))
    if lattice_um is not None:
        bases = [
            tuple(np.round(np.asarray(v, dtype=float) / dbu).astype(np.int64) for v in lattice_um)
        ]
    else:
        reference = max(corners.values(), key=len)
        bases = _candidate_bases(reference)
        if not bases:
            raise ValueError(
                "cannot infer the lattice: the pattern does not repeat in two directions. "
                "Pass period_um or lattice_um, or draw at least two cells each way."
            )

    found, overlapping = None, None
    for a1, a2 in bases:
        split = _complete_lattices(groups, corners, a1, a2)
        if split is None:
            continue
        counts, motif = split
        origin = np.min([first for _, first in motif], axis=0)
        drawn = {(_shape_key(points), tuple(points.min(axis=0))) for points in polygons}
        rebuilt = {
            (_shape_key(points), tuple(first + i * a1 + j * a2))
            for points, first in motif
            for i in range(counts[0])
            for j in range(counts[1])
        }
        if drawn != rebuilt or len(polygons) != len(motif) * counts[0] * counts[1]:
            continue
        if _overlaps(tuple(points - origin for points, _ in motif), a1, a2):
            overlapping = overlapping or (a1, a2)
            continue
        found = (a1, a2, counts, motif, origin)
        break
    if found is None and overlapping is not None:
        a1, a2 = overlapping
        raise ValueError(
            f"shapes on layer {layer} overlap (within a cell or across its edges) on the lattice "
            f"{tuple(a1 * dbu)}, {tuple(a2 * dbu)} µm; the solver needs non-overlapping shapes"
        )
    if found is None:
        described = "the given lattice" if lattice_um is not None else "any lattice inferred"
        raise ValueError(
            f"the pattern on layer {layer} does not fill a complete lattice at {described}: it "
            "is not one motif repeated on a periodic array. If a cell repeats a shape, pass "
            "period_um or lattice_um"
        )
    a1, a2, counts, motif, origin = found
    cell_polygons = tuple((points - origin) for points, _ in motif)

    rectangular = a1[1] == 0 and a2[0] == 0
    return UnitCell(
        period_um=(a1[0] * dbu, a2[1] * dbu) if rectangular else None,
        polygons=tuple(p.astype(float) * dbu for p in cell_polygons),
        n_cells=counts,
        origin_um=(float(origin[0] * dbu), float(origin[1] * dbu)),
        lattice_um=None if rectangular else (tuple(a1 * dbu), tuple(a2 * dbu)),
    )

PCell: the polygons of one cell, repeated n_cells times on a lattice.

The lattice is rectangular at period_um, or given by its primitive vectors lattice_um = ((a1x, a1y), (a2x, a2y)) -- e.g. a hexagonal one, ((a, 0), (a/2, a·√3/2)). The lattice vectors and every vertex are snapped to the layout grid (the database unit), so every cell drawn is an exact translate of the first; the snapped values are in component.info and are what :func:extract_unit_cell recovers. Pass polygon vertices as nested tuples (a PCell's arguments must be hashable), e.g. tuple(map(tuple, rcwa2d.ellipse(...).tolist())).

@gf.cell
def periodic_array(
    period_um: tuple[float, float] = (1.0, 1.0),
    polygons: tuple[tuple[tuple[float, float], ...], ...] = (
        ((0.25, 0.25), (0.75, 0.25), (0.75, 0.75), (0.25, 0.75)),
    ),
    n_cells: tuple[int, int] = (10, 10),
    layer: gf.typings.LayerSpec = (1, 0),
    lattice_um: tuple[tuple[float, float], tuple[float, float]] | None = None,
) -> gf.Component:
    """PCell: the ``polygons`` of one cell, repeated ``n_cells`` times on a lattice.

    The lattice is rectangular at ``period_um``, or given by its primitive
    vectors ``lattice_um = ((a1x, a1y), (a2x, a2y))`` -- e.g. a hexagonal one,
    ``((a, 0), (a/2, a·√3/2))``. The lattice vectors and every vertex are
    snapped to the layout grid (the database unit), so every cell drawn is an
    exact translate of the first; the snapped values are in ``component.info``
    and are what :func:`extract_unit_cell` recovers. Pass polygon vertices as
    nested tuples (a PCell's arguments must be hashable), e.g.
    ``tuple(map(tuple, rcwa2d.ellipse(...).tolist()))``.
    """
    component = gf.Component()
    dbu = component.kcl.dbu
    if lattice_um is None:
        lattice_um = ((period_um[0], 0.0), (0.0, period_um[1]))
    a1, a2 = (np.round(np.asarray(v, dtype=float) / dbu).astype(int) for v in lattice_um)
    if a1[0] * a2[1] - a1[1] * a2[0] == 0:
        raise ValueError(f"lattice {lattice_um} is degenerate on this grid")
    snapped = [np.round(np.asarray(polygon, dtype=float) / dbu).astype(int) for polygon in polygons]
    for i in range(n_cells[0]):
        for j in range(n_cells[1]):
            for vertices in snapped:
                shifted = (vertices + i * a1 + j * a2) * dbu
                component.add_polygon([tuple(v) for v in shifted], layer=layer)
    rectangular = a1[1] == 0 and a2[0] == 0
    component.info["period_um"] = (a1[0] * dbu, a2[1] * dbu) if rectangular else None
    component.info["lattice_um"] = (tuple(a1 * dbu), tuple(a2 * dbu))
    component.info["n_cells"] = tuple(n_cells)
    component.info["polygons"] = tuple(_as_vertices(v * dbu) for v in snapped)
    return component

Parameters:

    A material specification or :class:Oriented. An oriented crystal is cut first, then turned by rotation_deg: a layer's twist turns the crystal as cut.

  • wavelength_um (Array) –

  • rotation_deg (Sequence, default: (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) ) –

    Payload-style (rotationX, rotationY, rotationZ), degrees.

def material_tensor(
    spec: MaterialSpec | Oriented,
    wavelength_um: jax.Array,
    rotation_deg: Sequence = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
) -> jax.Array:
    """Lab-frame permittivity tensor ``[..., 3, 3]`` for a material specification.

    Args:
        spec: A material specification or :class:`Oriented`. An oriented
            crystal is cut first, then turned by ``rotation_deg``: a layer's
            twist turns the crystal as cut.
        wavelength_um: Vacuum wavelength in µm; differentiable.
        rotation_deg: Payload-style ``(rotationX, rotationY, rotationZ)``, degrees.
    """
    if isinstance(spec, Oriented):
        base = material_tensor(spec.material, wavelength_um)
        rotated = _rotate(base, spec.rotation_deg)
        return _rotate(rotated, rotation_deg)
    if isinstance(spec, str):
        _check_range(spec, wavelength_um)
        tensor = dispersion.at_wavelength(spec, wavelength_um)
    elif callable(spec):
        tensor = jnp.asarray(spec(wavelength_um))
    else:
        tensor = jnp.asarray(spec, dtype=complex)
    if tensor.ndim < 2 or tensor.shape[-2:] != (3, 3):  # an isotropic ε
        tensor = tensor[..., None, None] * jnp.eye(3)
    tensor = jnp.broadcast_to(tensor, jnp.shape(wavelength_um) + (3, 3)).astype(complex)
    return _rotate(tensor, rotation_deg)

def x_cut(axis_azimuth_deg: float = 0.0) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Optic axis in the wafer plane at ``axis_azimuth_deg`` from the layout x axis.

    An x- or y-cut wafer of a uniaxial crystal such as LiNbO₃: which of the two
    only matters for biaxial crystals. For a waveguide along layout y, TE light
    (E along x) sees the extraordinary index when ``axis_azimuth_deg = 0``.

    lattice_um,

    ambient=1.0,
    *,
    sidewall_slices=0,
