def structure_smatrix(structure) -> bcm.PlanarSMatrix:
    """The four-port S-matrix of an executed payload, on its scenario grid.

    ``Structure.execute`` computes the response to light from the incident side
    only: 8 of the 16 entries. A SAX circuit also needs light arriving from
    below, so the whole matrix is built here from the executed structure's own
    layer tensors and thicknesses, with the JAX solver (which matches the NumPy
    engine to ~1e-14). Its incident-side entries are the engine's r and t,
    scaled by √(kz_out / kz_in).

    Args:
        structure: A :class:`~hyperbolic_optics.structure.Structure` after
            ``execute``, ending in a ``Semi Infinite Isotropic Layer``.

    Returns:
        :class:`~hyperbolic_optics.bcm.PlanarSMatrix` with ``s`` shaped
        ``[A, B, F, T, 4, 4]``: the canonical axes (incident angle, azimuth,
        frequency, swept thickness), each of size 1 where the scenario does not
        sweep it. The azimuth is already in the tensors, and ``kx`` comes from
        the incident angle in the prism.
    """
    from hyperbolic_optics.layers import IsotropicSemiInfiniteLayer

    if structure.k_0 is None:
        raise ValueError("execute the structure first")
    exit_layer = structure.layers[-1]
    if not isinstance(exit_layer, IsotropicSemiInfiniteLayer):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"the exit is a {type(exit_layer).__name__}; the S-matrix needs an isotropic, "
            "lossless exit half-space (a Semi Infinite Isotropic Layer)"
        )
    layers = structure.layers[1:-1]
    thickness_um = [jnp.asarray(layer.thickness) * 1e4 for layer in layers]  # cm -> µm
    grid = jnp.broadcast_shapes(
        jnp.shape(structure.k_x),
        jnp.shape(structure.k_0),
        *(jnp.shape(layer.eps_tensor)[:-2] for layer in layers),
        *(jnp.shape(layer.mu_tensor)[:-2] for layer in layers),
        *(jnp.shape(d) for d in thickness_um),
    )

    def stacked(tensors):
        if not tensors:
            return jnp.zeros(grid + (0, 3, 3), dtype=complex)
        return jnp.stack([jnp.broadcast_to(jnp.asarray(t), grid + (3, 3)) for t in tensors], -3)

    eps = stacked([layer.eps_tensor for layer in layers])
    mu = stacked([layer.mu_tensor for layer in layers])
    thickness = (
        jnp.stack([jnp.broadcast_to(d, grid) for d in thickness_um], -1)
        if layers
        else jnp.zeros(grid + (0,))
    )
    wavelength_um = jnp.broadcast_to(2 * jnp.pi / jnp.asarray(structure.k_0) * 1e4, grid)
    kx = jnp.broadcast_to(jnp.real(jnp.asarray(structure.k_x)), grid)
    return bcm.stack_smatrix(
        eps, thickness, wavelength_um, kx, float(structure.eps_prism),
        float(exit_layer.eps_exit), mu=mu,
    )  # fmt: skip

docs.title: scattering
docs.text:
Numerically-stable scattering-matrix backend.

The default engine multiplies per-layer transfer matrices Mᵢ = Vᵢ·Pᵢ·Vᵢ⁻¹ with Pᵢ = diag(exp(-i·kz·k₀·d)) (waves.get_matrix). For thick / lossy / strongly-evanescent layers the propagation diagonal mixes exponentially growing and decaying terms, so the products overflow and lose precision (energy conservation drifts, eventually NaN).

This module reformulates the same 4×4 anisotropic problem as a scattering matrix cascaded with the Redheffer star product, where every propagation factor is a decaying exponential (exp(-|Im(kz)|·k₀·d) ≤ 1) — the growing matrices are never materialised — so it is stable in all cases. It is the opt-in backend behind Structure.execute(payload, backend="scattering") and produces the same reflection/transmission coefficients as the transfer method where both are well-conditioned, and correct coefficients where the transfer method fails.

Algorithm and conventions follow PyLlama (Bay, Lafait & Lequime / Bay et al., J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 39, 1431 (2022); arXiv:2012.05945), eqs 18-28, adapted to this codebase's field-vector ordering [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy] and partial-wave sort (WaveProfile.tangential_modes: columns [t0, t1, r0, r1] = forward, forward, backward, backward). Per-medium eigenvectors come from each layer's profile (interior layers and a semi-infinite crystal exit) or from the ambient dynamical matrices A_inc / A_exit (prism, isotropic exit).

scattering_interface_fields(layers, k_0, a_p, a_s)

Tangential field [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy] at the top of each layer, stably.

The transfer route to these fields propagates Gᵢ = Mᵢ·G_{i+1} through the per-layer matrices, which carry the growing exponentials this module exists to avoid. Here the mode amplitudes come out of the cascade instead and the field is rebuilt from each medium's own eigenvectors, so no growing term is ever formed.

For layer i, split the stack at its top interface into the cascade above it (L) and the cascade below (R). The forward amplitude entering the layer and the backward amplitude returning into it satisfy

c_f = L₀₀·a + L₀₁·c_b ,   c_b = R₁₀·c_f

-- the layer is illuminated from above by a and from below by whatever the rest of the stack sends back -- giving c_f = (I − L₀₁·R₁₀)⁻¹·L₀₀·a. The field is then P·[c_f, c_b].

Parameters:

  • layers (list) –

    The executed structure's layers.

  • k_0 (ndarray) –

    Canonical free-space wavenumber.

  • a_p (complex) –

    Incident forward p amplitude.

  • a_s (complex) –

    Incident forward s amplitude.

Returns:

  • list[ndarray] –

    One [..., 4] field array per layer, ordered prism-first, matching the

  • list[ndarray] –

    convention of :mod:hyperbolic_optics.fields.

def scattering_interface_fields(
    layers: list, k_0: np.ndarray, a_p: complex, a_s: complex
) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """Tangential field ``[Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy]`` at the top of each layer, stably.

    The transfer route to these fields propagates ``Gᵢ = Mᵢ·G_{i+1}`` through the
    per-layer matrices, which carry the growing exponentials this module exists
    to avoid. Here the mode amplitudes come out of the cascade instead and the
    field is rebuilt from each medium's own eigenvectors, so no growing term is
    ever formed.

    For layer ``i``, split the stack at its top interface into the cascade above
    it (``L``) and the cascade below (``R``). The forward amplitude entering the
    layer and the backward amplitude returning into it satisfy

        c_f = L₀₀·a + L₀₁·c_b ,   c_b = R₁₀·c_f

    -- the layer is illuminated from above by ``a`` and from below by whatever
    the rest of the stack sends back -- giving
    ``c_f = (I − L₀₁·R₁₀)⁻¹·L₀₀·a``. The field is then ``P·[c_f, c_b]``.

    Args:
        layers: The executed structure's layers.
        k_0: Canonical free-space wavenumber.
        a_p: Incident forward p amplitude.
        a_s: Incident forward s amplitude.

    Returns:
        One ``[..., 4]`` field array per layer, ordered prism-first, matching the
        convention of :mod:`hyperbolic_optics.fields`.
    """
    media = [_medium(layer) for layer in layers]
    count = len(media)
    interfaces = [
        _interface_scattering(media[i][0], media[i][1], media[i][2], media[i + 1][0], k_0)
        for i in range(count - 1)
    ]

    # below[i] cascades interfaces i .. end; above[i] cascades 0 .. i-1.
    below: list[np.ndarray | None] = [None] * count
    accumulated = None
    for i in range(count - 2, -1, -1):
        accumulated = interfaces[i] if accumulated is None else _star(interfaces[i], accumulated)
        below[i] = accumulated

    above: list[np.ndarray | None] = [None] * count
    accumulated = None
    for i in range(1, count):
        accumulated = (
            interfaces[i - 1] if accumulated is None else _star(accumulated, interfaces[i - 1])
        )
        above[i] = accumulated

    # Ambient columns are reordered to [p_fwd, s_fwd, ...], so the incident
    # forward pair is (p, s) in that order.
    reference = interfaces[0][..., 0, 0]
    incident = np.stack(
        [np.full_like(reference, a_p), np.full_like(reference, a_s)], axis=-1
    )  # [..., 2]

    identity = np.eye(2, dtype=np.complex128)
    fields = []
    for i in range(count):
        if above[i] is None:  # the prism: nothing above it to correct for
            forward = incident
        else:
            l00, l01 = above[i][..., :2, :2], above[i][..., :2, 2:]
            forward = l00 @ incident[..., np.newaxis]
            if below[i] is not None:
                r10 = below[i][..., 2:, :2]
                forward = np.linalg.inv(identity - l01 @ r10) @ forward
            forward = forward[..., 0]

        if below[i] is None:  # the exit half-space carries no backward wave
            backward = np.zeros_like(forward)
        else:
            backward = (below[i][..., 2:, :2] @ forward[..., np.newaxis])[..., 0]

        # The prism's incident amplitude carries only the batch axes of its own
        # interface; the backward wave returned by the cascade below carries
        # them all. A non-dispersive first layer has no F axis, so the two
        # differ on a frequency sweep and must be broadcast before joining.
        forward, backward = np.broadcast_arrays(forward, backward)
        amplitudes = np.concatenate([forward, backward], axis=-1)  # [..., 4]
        fields.append((media[i][0] @ amplitudes[..., np.newaxis])[..., 0])

    return fields

Reflection coefficients are in the prism's s/p basis. def scattering_coefficients(layers: list, k_0: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Reflection/transmission coefficients via the stable scattering-matrix method.

    Args:
        layers: The executed structure's layers (``structure.layers``), each
            exposing eigenvectors via ``profile`` or an ambient dynamical matrix.
        k_0: Canonical free-space wavenumber ``[1, 1, F, 1]``.

    Returns:
        Dict of the eight complex coefficients ``r_pp, r_ss, r_ps, r_sp, t_pp,
        t_ss, t_ps, t_sp`` in canonical ``[A, B, F, T]`` layout (un-presented).

    Note:
        Reflection coefficients are in the prism's s/p basis. For an isotropic
        exit the transmission coefficients are too; for a semi-infinite
        anisotropic exit they name that crystal's eigenmodes, ordered p-like
        first to match the prism -- the same convention the transfer backend
        uses, so the two agree coefficient for coefficient.
    """
    media = [_medium(layer) for layer in layers]
    scattering = None
    for (p_left, q_left, d_left), (p_right, _, _) in zip(media[:-1], media[1:], strict=True):
        interface = _interface_scattering(p_left, q_left, d_left, p_right, k_0)
        scattering = interface if scattering is None else _star(scattering, interface)

    assert_canonical(scattering, matrix_ndim=2, name="scattering_matrix")
    s = scattering
    # PyLlama r_kj is (out k, in j); this codebase uses r_{in->out}, so the cross
    # terms transpose (verified against the transfer backend).
    return {
        "r_pp": s[..., 2, 0],
        "r_ss": s[..., 3, 1],
        "r_ps": s[..., 3, 0],
        "r_sp": s[..., 2, 1],
        "t_pp": s[..., 0, 0],
        "t_ss": s[..., 1, 1],
        "t_ps": s[..., 1, 0],
        "t_sp": s[..., 0, 1],
    }

Simulation scenario configuration and setup.

This module defines four scenario types for different analysis needs:

  1. Simple: Single-point calculation (scalar angles and frequency)
  2. Incident: Angle sweep at multiple frequencies (kx-ω plots)
  3. Azimuthal: Sample rotation at fixed incident angle (β-ω plots)
  4. Dispersion: k-space map at fixed frequency (kx-ky plots)

Each scenario type automatically sets up appropriate angle and frequency arrays with correct dimensions for batch processing.

def __init__(self, data: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Initialize scenario configuration for simulation.

    Args:
        data: Dictionary with 'type' and scenario-specific parameters

    Raises:
        NotImplementedError: If scenario type is not recognized

    Example:
        >>> data = {"type": "Simple", "incidentAngle": 45.0,
        ...         "azimuthal_angle": 0.0, "frequency": 1460.0}
        >>> scenario = ScenarioSetup(data)
    """
    _validate_scenario_keys(data)
    self.data = data
    self.type = data.get("type")
    self.incident_angle = data.get("incidentAngle", None)
    self.azimuthal_angle = data.get("azimuthal_angle", None)
    self.frequency = data.get("frequency", None)
    self.create_scenario()

def create_scenario(self) -> None:
    """Create scenario-specific angle and frequency arrays.

    Dispatches to appropriate scenario creation method based on type.

    Raises:
        NotImplementedError: If scenario type is not implemented
    """
    if self.type == "Incident":
        self.create_incident_scenario()
    elif self.type == "Azimuthal":
        self.create_azimuthal_scenario()
    elif self.type == "Dispersion":
        self.create_dispersion_scenario()
    elif self.type == "Simple":
        self.create_simple_scenario()
    elif self.type == "FullSweep":
        self.create_full_sweep_scenario()
    else:
        raise NotImplementedError(f"Scenario type {self.type} not implemented")

def create_azimuthal_scenario(self) -> None:
    """Create azimuthal rotation scenario at fixed incident angle.

    Rotates the sample through 360 azimuthal angles (0 to 2π) while
    maintaining constant incident angle.

    Note:
        Useful for studying in-plane anisotropy and rotational symmetry.
        incidentAngle must be provided in input data.
    """
    self.incident_angle = np.float64(m.radians(self.incident_angle))
    self.azimuthal_angle = self._angle_axis(
        self.azimuthal_angle,
        "azimuthal_angle",

    )

def create_dispersion_scenario(self) -> None:
    """Create k-space dispersion scenario at fixed frequency.

    Sets up grid of incident angles (180 points) and azimuthal angles
    (480 points) for mapping isofrequency contours in kx-ky space.

    Note:
        Requires 'frequency' to be specified in input data.
        Generates data for kx vs ky momentum-space plots.

    self.incident_angle = self._angle_axis(
        self.incident_angle, "incidentAngle", 1.0e-8, m.pi / 2.0 - 1.0e-8, 180, "polar_points"
    )
    self.azimuthal_angle = self._angle_axis(
        self.azimuthal_angle,
        "azimuthal_angle",
        1.0e-5,
        2.0 * m.pi - 1.0e-5,
        480,
        "azimuthal_points",
    )

    self.frequency = float(self.frequency)

docs.title: structure
docs.text:
Main simulation structure and workflow orchestration.

The Structure class is the primary interface for running optical simulations. It coordinates the entire calculation workflow:

  1. Parse scenario configuration
  2. Create multilayer stack
  3. Calculate transfer matrices for each layer
  4. Multiply matrices to get total system response
  5. Extract reflection coefficients

The transfer matrix method is a recursive approach where each layer's effect is represented by a 4×4 matrix relating field components at its boundaries. The total response is the product of all layer matrices.

Reference: Passler & Paarmann, JOSA B 34, 2128-2139 (2017)

Classes:

  • Structure –

    Main interface for optical simulations.

Structure()

Main interface for optical simulations.

Examples:

Basic single-point calculation:

>>> payload = {
...     "ScenarioData": {
...         "type": "Simple",
...         "incidentAngle": 45.0,
...         "azimuthal_angle": 0.0,
...         "frequency": 1460.0
...     },
...     "Layers": [
...         {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
...         {"type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
...          "material": "Calcite", "rotationY": 90}
...     ]
... }
>>> structure = Structure()
>>> structure.execute(payload)
>>> print(f"R_pp = {abs(structure.r_pp)**2:.4f}")

Multi-layer structure with air gap:

>>> payload = {
...     "ScenarioData": {"type": "Incident"},
...     "Layers": [
...         {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
...         {"type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer",
...          "thickness": 0.5, "permittivity": 1.0},
...         {"type": "Crystal Layer", "material": "Quartz",
...          "thickness": 1.0, "rotationY": 70},
...         {"type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
...          "material": "Sapphire", "rotationY": 90}
...     ]
... }
>>> structure = Structure()
>>> structure.execute(payload)
>>> # Results are arrays: structure.r_pp.shape = (410, 360)

Custom material with complex permittivity:

>>> custom_material = {
...     "eps_xx": {"real": 2.5, "imag": 0.1},
...     "eps_yy": {"real": 3.0, "imag": 0.05},
...     "eps_zz": {"real": -4.0, "imag": 0.5}
... }
>>> payload = {
...     "ScenarioData": {"type": "Simple", "incidentAngle": 45.0,
...                      "azimuthal_angle": 0.0, "frequency": 1000.0},
...     "Layers": [
...         {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 25.0},
...         {"type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
...          "material": custom_material, "rotationY": 45}
...     ]
... }
>>> structure = Structure()
>>> structure.execute(payload)

def resolve_frequency(self, layer_data_list: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> np.ndarray:
    """Resolve the frequency array (cm⁻¹) for the simulation.

    Precedence: an explicit ``ScenarioData['frequency']`` (scalar or list)
    wins; otherwise fall back to the default range of the *last
    material-bearing layer* (the bulk crystal — an isotropic exit layer has
    no dispersive range, so it is skipped automatically).

    Args:
        layer_data_list: The raw layer configuration dicts.

    Returns:
        A 1-D frequency array (length 1 for single-frequency scenarios).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If no frequency is given and no material can supply a range.
    """
    if self.frequency is not None:
        return np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(self.frequency, dtype=np.float64))
    for layer in reversed(layer_data_list):
        material = layer.get("material")
        if material is not None:
            freq = create_material(material).frequency
            if freq is not None:
                return np.asarray(freq, dtype=np.float64)
    raise ValueError(
        "No frequency given and no dispersive material to derive a range from; "
        "set ScenarioData['frequency']."
    )

Calculate parallel wavevector and free-space wavenumber.

Computes

kx = n_prism · sin(θ) where n_prism = √ε_prism k0 = ω / c = 2π · frequency

Note

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/structure.py 
def calculate_kx_k0(self) -> None:
    """Calculate parallel wavevector and free-space wavenumber.

    Computes:
        kx = n_prism · sin(θ) where n_prism = √ε_prism
        k0 = ω / c = 2π · frequency

    Note:
        kx is conserved across all interfaces (phase matching condition).
    """
    incident_angle = np.asarray(self.incident_angle, dtype=np.float64)
    kx = np.sqrt(np.float64(self.eps_prism)) * np.sin(incident_angle)
    # Canonical layout (see hyperbolic_optics.axes): kx lives on the A axis,
    # k0 on the F axis; all other batch axes (incl. thickness T) are size 1.
    # A swept layer introduces T>1 via broadcasting, so neither needs to know
    # about it here.
    self.k_x = canonicalize(np.atleast_1d(kx).astype(np.float64), batch_axes=(A,))
    k0 = np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(self.frequency, dtype=np.float64)) * 2.0 * m.pi
    self.k_0 = canonicalize(k0, batch_axes=(F,))
    # Boundary-in: kx and k0 enter the pipeline canonical [A, 1, 1] / [1, 1, F].
    assert_canonical(self.k_x, matrix_ndim=0, name="kx")
    assert_canonical(self.k_0, matrix_ndim=0, name="k0")

def get_layers(self, layer_data_list: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
    """Create all layers in the structure from configuration.

    Args:
        layer_data_list: List of layer configuration dictionaries

    Note:
        First layer must be Ambient Incident Layer (prism).
        Automatically determines frequency range if not specified.
    """
    # First Layer is prism, so we parse it
    self.eps_prism = layer_data_list[0].get("permittivity", None)
    self._validate_thickness_sweep(layer_data_list)
    # Resolve the frequency array once and share it with the scenario so
    # every layer evaluates its material over the same frequencies.
    self.frequency = self.resolve_frequency(layer_data_list)
    self._warn_frequency_out_of_range(layer_data_list)
    self.scenario.frequency = self.frequency
    self.calculate_kx_k0()

    # Create prism layer and add it to layers list
    self.layers.append(
        self.factory.create_layer(
            layer_data_list[0],
            self.scenario,
            self.k_x,
            self.k_0,
        )
    )

    # Create the rest of the layers and add them to layers list
    for layer_data in layer_data_list[1:]:
        self.layers.append(
            self.factory.create_layer(
                layer_data,
                self.scenario,
                self.k_x,
                self.k_0,
            )
        )

Calculate total transfer matrix by multiplying layer matrices.

Performs matrix multiplication of all layer transfer matrices from incident to exit medium: M_total = M_exit · ... · M_2 · M_1 · M_prism

def calculate(self) -> None:
    """Calculate total transfer matrix by multiplying layer matrices.

    Performs matrix multiplication of all layer transfer matrices from
    incident to exit medium: M_total = M_exit · ... · M_2 · M_1 · M_prism

    Note:
        Uses functools.reduce with operator.matmul for efficient
        sequential multiplication.
    """
    transfer_matrices = [layer.matrix for layer in self.layers]
    self.transfer_matrix = functools.reduce(operator.matmul, transfer_matrices)

calculate_reflectivity(stabilize=True)

Extract reflection coefficients from total transfer matrix.

Parameters:

  • stabilize (bool, default: True ) –

    Recompute any batch point whose 2x2 minors cancelled to the rounding floor using the scattering cascade. Pass False for the literal transfer-matrix result.

Solves the system of equations to obtain r_pp, r_ss, r_ps, r_sp from the boundary conditions encoded in the transfer matrix.

Note

Reflection coefficients are complex and relate incident field amplitudes to reflected field amplitudes: E_reflected = r · E_incident

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/structure.py 
def calculate_reflectivity(self, stabilize: bool = True) -> None:
    """Extract reflection coefficients from total transfer matrix.

    Args:
        stabilize: Recompute any batch point whose 2x2 minors cancelled to
            the rounding floor using the scattering cascade. Pass ``False``
            for the literal transfer-matrix result.

    Solves the system of equations to obtain r_pp, r_ss, r_ps, r_sp
    from the boundary conditions encoded in the transfer matrix.

    Note:
        Reflection coefficients are complex and relate incident field
        amplitudes to reflected field amplitudes:
        E_reflected = r · E_incident
    """
    # Boundary-out: the assembled transfer matrix is canonical [A, B, F, 4, 4].
    assert_canonical(self.transfer_matrix, matrix_ndim=2, name="transfer_matrix")
    t = self.transfer_matrix
    bottom_line, bottom_trust = _minor(t[..., 0, 0] * t[..., 2, 2], t[..., 0, 2] * t[..., 2, 0])
    pp, pp_trust = _minor(t[..., 0, 0] * t[..., 3, 2], t[..., 3, 0] * t[..., 0, 2])
    ps, ps_trust = _minor(t[..., 0, 0] * t[..., 1, 2], t[..., 1, 0] * t[..., 0, 2])
    sp, sp_trust = _minor(t[..., 3, 0] * t[..., 2, 2], t[..., 3, 2] * t[..., 2, 0])
    ss, ss_trust = _minor(t[..., 1, 0] * t[..., 2, 2], t[..., 1, 2] * t[..., 2, 0])

    self.r_pp = pp / bottom_line
    self.r_ps = ps / bottom_line
    self.r_sp = sp / bottom_line
    self.r_ss = ss / bottom_line

    # Every coefficient is a 2x2 minor over a denominator. A layer carrying a
    # growing exponential drives the assembled matrix towards rank 1, where
    # all such minors vanish analytically -- so each is computed as the
    # difference of two nearly equal products. r_pp and r_ss survive that
    # because their numerator and the denominator lose precision together and
    # the error cancels in the ratio. A coefficient that is zero by symmetry
    # has no such partner: its numerator cancels all the way to the rounding
    # floor and what is left is noise, returned as a confident 1e-2.
    #
    # _minor reports how much of each subtraction survived, so the points
    # where that has happened are known exactly rather than guessed at.
    self._minor_trust = np.minimum.reduce(
        [bottom_trust, pp_trust, ps_trust, sp_trust, ss_trust]
    )
    if stabilize:
        self._repair_lost_minors()

    # Boundary-out (single presentation rule, see canonical-shape plan 4.6):
    # coefficients are canonical [A, B, F]; reorder to (F, A, B) then squeeze
    # the size-1 axes. This reproduces every scenario's historical output
    # shape (Incident/Azimuthal -> (F, angle); Dispersion -> (A, B);
    # FullSweep -> (F, A, B); Simple -> scalar).
    self.r_pp = self._present(self.r_pp)
    self.r_ps = self._present(self.r_ps)
    self.r_sp = self._present(self.r_sp)
    self.r_ss = self._present(self.r_ss)

docs.text:
calculate_transmissivity()

Extract transmission amplitude coefficients from the transfer matrix.

Computes t_pp, t_ps, t_sp, t_ss. The results are returned in the same presentation layout as the reflection coefficients (see :meth:_present), so t_* and r_* share axis ordering. Not called by execute() by default — invoke explicitly after calculate() if transmission is needed.

Note

These are bare amplitude coefficients. For power transmittance, layer-resolved absorption, and field profiles computed numerically from the propagated fields (energy-conserving R + T + ΣA = 1), use :class:hyperbolic_optics.fields.FieldProfile, which is the blessed path.

Source code in hyperbolic_optics/structure.py 
def calculate_transmissivity(self) -> None:
    """Extract transmission *amplitude* coefficients from the transfer matrix.

    Computes ``t_pp, t_ps, t_sp, t_ss``. The results are returned in the same
    presentation layout as the reflection coefficients (see :meth:`_present`),
    so ``t_*`` and ``r_*`` share axis ordering. Not called by ``execute()`` by
    default — invoke explicitly after ``calculate()`` if transmission is needed.

    Note:
        These are bare amplitude coefficients. For *power* transmittance,
        layer-resolved absorption, and field profiles computed numerically
        from the propagated fields (energy-conserving ``R + T + ΣA = 1``), use
        :class:`hyperbolic_optics.fields.FieldProfile`, which is the blessed path.
    """
    bottom_line = (
        self.transfer_matrix[..., 0, 0] * self.transfer_matrix[..., 2, 2]
        - self.transfer_matrix[..., 0, 2] * self.transfer_matrix[..., 2, 0]
    )
    self.t_pp = self._present(self.transfer_matrix[..., 0, 0] / bottom_line)
    self.t_ps = self._present(-self.transfer_matrix[..., 0, 2] / bottom_line)
    self.t_sp = self._present(-self.transfer_matrix[..., 2, 0] / bottom_line)
    self.t_ss = self._present(self.transfer_matrix[..., 2, 2] / bottom_line)

def calculate_scattering(self) -> None:
    """Fill reflection/transmission coefficients via the scattering backend.

    Uses :func:`hyperbolic_optics.scattering.scattering_coefficients` — a
    numerically-stable Redheffer scattering-matrix cascade built from each
    layer's eigenmodes — instead of the transfer-matrix product. Sets
    ``r_pp … t_ss`` in the same presentation layout as
    :meth:`calculate_reflectivity`.
    """
    coefficients = scattering_coefficients(self.layers, self.k_0)
    for name, value in coefficients.items():
        setattr(self, name, present(value))

"Layers": [ ... {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0}, ... {"type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer", ... def execute(self, payload: dict[str, Any], backend: str = "transfer") -> None:
    """Execute complete simulation from configuration payload.

    Args:
        payload: Dictionary with 'ScenarioData' and 'Layers' keys.
        backend: ``"transfer"`` (default) for the 4×4 transfer-matrix product,
            or ``"scattering"`` for the numerically-stable scattering-matrix
            backend (correct for thick / lossy / strongly-evanescent stacks
            where the transfer product overflows). Both yield the same
            coefficients where the transfer method is well-conditioned.

    Example:
        >>> payload = {
        ...     "ScenarioData": {"type": "Simple", "incidentAngle": 45.0,
        ...                      "azimuthal_angle": 0.0, "frequency": 1460.0},
        ...     "Layers": [
        ...         {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
        ...         {"type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
        ...          "material": "Calcite", "rotationY": 90}
        ...     ]
        ... }
        >>> structure = Structure()
        >>> structure.execute(payload)
        >>> R_pp = abs(structure.r_pp)**2
    """
    if backend not in ("transfer", "scattering"):
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown backend {backend!r}; use 'transfer' or 'scattering'.")

    self._reset()

    # Get the scenario data
    self.get_scenario(payload.get("ScenarioData"))

    if backend == "scattering":
        # The per-layer transfer matrices built in get_layers can overflow for
        # thick/evanescent layers -- harmless here, since the scattering
        # backend reads each layer's eigenmodes (profile), not its matrix. The
        # errstate silences that expected overflow (the scattering engine
        # itself never forms a growing exponential).
        with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            self.get_layers(payload.get("Layers", None))
            self.calculate_scattering()
        self.backend = backend
        return

    # Get the layers (builds each layer's eigenmodes / matrices)
    self.get_layers(payload.get("Layers", None))

    # Calculate the transfer matrix
    self.calculate()

    # Calculate the reflectivity
    self.calculate_reflectivity()
    self.backend = backend
    self._warn_if_ill_conditioned()

docs.title: sweep
docs.text:
Sweep a single layer's thickness as an extra output dimension.

The canonical engine sweeps incident angle, azimuth, and frequency as the batch axes [A, B, F] (see :mod:hyperbolic_optics.axes). A layer's thickness is a per-layer property, not a scenario axis, so this helper sweeps it the pragmatic way: re-run the structure once per thickness and stack the results along a new leading index. Each run is cheap, and the output gains a thickness axis in front of the usual presentation shape — e.g. an Incident r_pp of shape (F, angle) becomes (n_thickness, F, angle).

This keeps the core convention untouched (no golden re-baseline). If you ever need thickness as a vectorized batch axis alongside angle/azimuth/frequency, that is a separate, larger change to the canonical layout.

Example

payload = { ... "ScenarioData": {"type": "Incident"}, ... "Layers": [ ... {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0}, ... {"type": "Crystal Layer", "material": "Calcite", ... "thickness": 1.0, "rotationY": 90}, ... {"type": "Semi Infinite Isotropic Layer", "permittivity": 1.0}, ... ], ... } sweep = ThicknessSweep(payload, layer_index=1, thicknesses=[0.5, 1.0, 2.0]) sweep.r_pp.shape # (3, F, angle) sweep.transmittance("p") # (3, F, angle) sweep.layer_absorption("p") # per-interior-layer, each (3, F, angle)

def __init__(
    self,
    payload: dict[str, Any],
    layer_index: int,
    thicknesses: np.ndarray | list[float],
) -> None:
    """Execute ``payload`` once per thickness for the chosen layer.

    Args:
        payload: A complete ``Structure.execute`` payload.
        layer_index: Index into ``payload["Layers"]`` of the layer to sweep;
            must be a finite layer (``Crystal Layer`` or ``Isotropic
            Middle-Stack Layer``).
        thicknesses: Thicknesses to sweep, in microns.

    Raises:
        IndexError: If ``layer_index`` is out of range.
        ValueError: If the selected layer has no sweepable thickness, or
            ``thicknesses`` is empty.
    """
    layers = payload.get("Layers", [])
    if not 0 <= layer_index < len(layers):
        raise IndexError(f"layer_index {layer_index} out of range (0..{len(layers) - 1}).")
    layer_type = layers[layer_index].get("type")
    if layer_type not in _THICKNESS_LAYERS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Layer {layer_index} ({layer_type!r}) has no sweepable thickness; "
            f"choose a finite layer of type {sorted(_THICKNESS_LAYERS)}."
        )
    self.thicknesses = np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(thicknesses, dtype=np.float64))
    if self.thicknesses.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("thicknesses must contain at least one value.")

    self.layer_index = layer_index
    self.layer_type = layer_type
    self.structures: list[Structure] = []
    for thickness in self.thicknesses:
        single = copy.deepcopy(payload)
        single["Layers"][layer_index]["thickness"] = float(thickness)
        structure = Structure()
        structure.execute(single)
        self.structures.append(structure)
    self._fields = [FieldProfile(structure) for structure in self.structures]

def layer_absorption(
    self, polarization: str | tuple[complex, complex] = "p"
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Per-interior-layer absorptance, each stacked over thickness.

    Returns a list (top->bottom) of ``{"index", "type", "absorptance"}`` where
    ``absorptance`` has a leading thickness axis. Empty when there are no finite
    interior layers. The swept layer's own absorptance varies with thickness.
    """
    per_run = [f.layer_absorption(polarization) for f in self._fields]
    stacked = []
    for entries in zip(*per_run, strict=True):
        stacked.append(
            {
                "index": entries[0]["index"],
                "type": entries[0]["type"],
                "absorptance": self._stack([e["absorptance"] for e in entries]),
            }
        )
    return stacked

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Basic Calcite Reflection Example

This script demonstrates the most basic usage of the hyperbolic-optics package
by calculating reflection coefficients for a simple Calcite crystal structure.
"""


import numpy as np

from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure


def main():
    """
    Calculate basic reflection coefficients for Calcite at a single frequency and angle.
    """
    print("=== Basic Calcite Reflection Example ===\n")

    # Define a simple structure with Calcite
    payload = {
        "ScenarioData": {
            "type": "Simple",
            "incidentAngle": 45.0,  # 45 degree incident angle
            "azimuthal_angle": 0.0,  # No azimuthal rotation
            "frequency": 1460.0,  # Frequency in cm^-1
        },
        "Layers": [
            {
                "type": "Ambient Incident Layer",
                "permittivity": 50.0,  # High-index prism
            },
            {
                "type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer",
                "thickness": 0.1,  # Thin air gap (in mm)
                "permittivity": 1.0,  # Air
            },
            {
                "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
                "material": "Calcite",
                "rotationX": 0,
                "rotationY": 90,  # Rotate optical axis
                "rotationZ": 0,
            },
        ],
    }

    # Create and execute the simulation
    print("Creating structure and calculating...")
    structure = Structure()
    structure.execute(payload)

    # For a Simple scenario the coefficients are 0-d complex arrays; convert to
    # Python complex so they format cleanly.
    r_pp, r_ss = complex(structure.r_pp), complex(structure.r_ss)
    r_ps, r_sp = complex(structure.r_ps), complex(structure.r_sp)

    def fmt(z: complex) -> str:
        return f"{z.real:+.6f} {z.imag:+.6f}j"

    incident_deg = float(np.degrees(structure.incident_angle))
    frequency = float(np.squeeze(structure.frequency))

    print("Results:")
    print(f"  Incident angle: {incident_deg:.1f} deg")
    print(f"  Frequency: {frequency:.1f} cm^-1")
    print("  Material: Calcite")
    print()
    print("Reflection coefficients:")
    print(f"  r_pp = {fmt(r_pp)}")
    print(f"  r_ss = {fmt(r_ss)}")
    print(f"  r_ps = {fmt(r_ps)}")
    print(f"  r_sp = {fmt(r_sp)}")
    print()
    print("Reflectivities (|r|^2):")
    print(f"  R_pp = {abs(r_pp) ** 2:.4f}")
    print(f"  R_ss = {abs(r_ss) ** 2:.4f}")
    print(f"  R_ps = {abs(r_ps) ** 2:.4f}")
    print(f"  R_sp = {abs(r_sp) ** 2:.4f}")
    print()
    print(f"Total p-polarized reflectivity: {abs(r_pp) ** 2 + abs(r_ps) ** 2:.4f}")
    print(f"Total s-polarized reflectivity: {abs(r_ss) ** 2 + abs(r_sp) ** 2:.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

                "thickness": 0.5,
                "permittivity": 1.0,
            },
            {
                "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
                "material": "Calcite",
                "rotationX": 0,
                "rotationY": 70,  # Optical axis tilt
                "rotationZ": 0,
            },
        ],
    }

    # Create and execute the simulation
    structure = Structure()
    structure.execute(payload)

    # Calculate total reflectivity
    R_total = abs(structure.r_pp) ** 2 + abs(structure.r_ps) ** 2

    # Plot removed for benchmarking
    print(f"Dispersion calculation complete. R_total shape: {R_total.shape}")

    plot_mueller_dispersion(structure, R_total)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Your First Simulation
docs.text:
Let's run a simple simulation to calculate reflection coefficients for a Calcite crystal.

from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure

# Define the structure
payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Simple",
        "incidentAngle": 45.0,      # degrees
        "azimuthal_angle": 0.0,      # degrees
        "frequency": 1460.0          # cm^-1
    },
    "Layers": [
        {
            "type": "Ambient Incident Layer",
            "permittivity": 50.0
        },
        {
            "type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer",
            "thickness": 0.1,  # mm
            "permittivity": 1.0
        },
        {
            "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
            "material": "Calcite",
            "rotationX": 0,
            "rotationY": 90,
            "rotationZ": 0
        }
    ]
}

# Run simulation
structure = Structure()
structure.execute(payload)

# Get reflection coefficients
r_pp = structure.r_pp  # p-to-p
r_ss = structure.r_ss  # s-to-s
r_ps = structure.r_ps  # p-to-s
r_sp = structure.r_sp  # s-to-p

# Calculate reflectivities
R_pp = abs(r_pp)**2
R_ss = abs(r_ss)**2

print(f"p-polarized reflectivity: {R_pp:.4f}")
print(f"s-polarized reflectivity: {R_ss:.4f}")

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The hyperbolic-optics package uses the 4×4 transfer matrix method to calculate reflection and transmission coefficients for multilayer anisotropic structures.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The Structure class is the main interface for setting up and running simulations. It:

  • Defines the geometry (layers and materials)
  • Sets up the scenario (angles, frequencies)
  • Calculates reflection coefficients

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
A structure consists of multiple layers:

  1. Ambient Incident Layer: The incident medium (e.g., prism)
  2. Middle Layers: Can be isotropic or anisotropic, finite thickness
  3. Exit Layer: Usually semi-infinite, can be isotropic or anisotropic

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Materials are defined by their permittivity (ε) and permeability (μ) tensors:

  • Uniaxial: Single optical axis (Quartz, Calcite, Sapphire)
  • Biaxial/Monoclinic: Two or three optical axes (Gallium Oxide)
  • Isotropic: No optical axis (Air, glass)
  • Arbitrary: Custom-defined tensors

docs.title: Reflection Coefficients
docs.text:
The package calculates four reflection coefficients:

  • r_pp: p-polarized → p-polarized
  • r_ss: s-polarized → s-polarized
  • r_ps: p-polarized → s-polarized
  • r_sp: s-polarized → p-polarized

Reflectivity is calculated as: \(R = |r|^2\)

docs.title: Transmission, Absorption & Field Profiles
docs.text:
Beyond reflection, FieldProfile reconstructs the electromagnetic field through the stack and derives power quantities numerically from the time-averaged Poynting flux \(S_z = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Re}(E_x H_y^* - E_y H_x^*)\) rather than from closed-form coefficients:

  • Transmittance \(T = S_z^{\text{exit}}/S_z^{\text{inc}}\)
  • Layer-resolved absorption \(A_i = [S_z(\text{top}_i) - S_z(\text{bottom}_i)]/S_z^{\text{inc}}\)
  • Field profiles \(E(z), H(z), S_z(z)\) through each layer

These conserve energy exactly: \(R + T + \sum_i A_i = 1\). For a single semi-infinite anisotropic exit there are no interior layers, so \(T = 1 - R\) is the power delivered into the bulk and the field profile shows it absorbed with depth (decay length set by \(\mathrm{Im}(k_z)\)).

References: Passler, Jeannin & Paarmann, J. Opt. Soc. Am. B 37, 1060 (2020).

docs.title: Coordinate System
docs.text:
• x-axis: Parallel to the interface, in the plane of incidence
  • y-axis: Parallel to the interface, perpendicular to plane of incidence
  • z-axis: Normal to the interface (propagation direction)

docs.title: Rotations
docs.text:
Materials can be rotated using Euler angles:

  • rotationY: Rotation around y-axis (often the optical axis tilt)
  • rotationZ: Rotation around z-axis (azimuthal rotation)

docs.title: Transfer Matrix Method
docs.text:
The 4×4 transfer matrix method tracks both electric and magnetic field components through each layer. For each layer:

  1. Calculate the Berreman matrix (describes wave propagation)
  2. Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors (wave modes)
  3. Construct the transfer matrix
  4. Multiply matrices for all layers
  5. Extract reflection coefficients

docs.title: Mueller Matrices
docs.text:
Mueller matrices describe how polarization states transform upon reflection:

\[\mathbf{S}_{out} = \mathbf{M} \cdot \mathbf{S}_{in}\]

Where \(\mathbf{S}\) is the Stokes vector: \([S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3]^T\)

The package can:

  1. Calculate Mueller matrices from reflection coefficients
  2. Simulate optical components (polarizers, wave plates)
  3. Calculate Stokes parameters and polarization properties

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• Frequency: cm⁻¹ (wavenumbers)
  • Thickness: mm (converted to cm internally)
  • Angles: degrees (converted to radians internally)
  • Permittivity/Permeability: dimensionless

docs.title: Crossed Gratings (2D RCWA)
docs.text:
hyperbolic_optics.rcwa2d computes diffraction by structures that are periodic in x and y on a rectangular lattice and layered in z: pillar and hole arrays, metasurfaces, photonic-crystal slabs. Each patterned layer is a background material and non-overlapping polygons, and every one of them can have a full 3×3 permittivity and permeability, including the xz and yz components of a tilted crystal axis. It is written in JAX with the same layer engine as the 1D grating solver, so jax.grad works with respect to:

  • geometry: every polygon vertex (so radii, widths, positions, rotations), thickness, period
  • materials and their orientation
  • wavelength and incidence

It needs the optional JAX dependency and 64-bit JAX.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
import jax.numpy as jnp
from hyperbolic_optics import bcm, rcwa2d

eye = jnp.eye(3, dtype=complex)
# LiNbO3 with the optic axis tilted 45° out of plane
crystal = jnp.diag(jnp.array([5.06, 5.46, 5.46], dtype=complex))
ln = bcm.rotate_tensor(crystal, bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, jnp.radians(45.0), 0.0))

fin = rcwa2d.Shape(rcwa2d.rectangle(center=(0.17, 0.17), size=(0.2, 0.1)), ln)
disc = rcwa2d.Shape(rcwa2d.ellipse(center=(0.17, 0.17), radii=(0.08, 0.08)), 2.1 * eye)
layers = [
    rcwa2d.PatternedLayer(0.30, eye, (fin,)),      # fins in air
    rcwa2d.PatternedLayer(0.05, 1.46**2 * eye, (disc,)),
    rcwa2d.uniform(2.1 * eye, 0.1),                # an unpatterned film
]
result = rcwa2d.solve_crossed_grating(
    layers, period_um=(0.34, 0.34), wavelength_um=0.55, incidence_rad=0.2,
    eps_incident=1.0, eps_exit=1.46**2, max_order=(5, 5),
)
result.orders        # [121, 2]: (m, n) of each order
result.T.shape       # (121, 2, 2): [order, out, in], 0 = p and 1 = s
  • Shapes. Shape(vertices, eps, mu=None) takes any simple polygon in µm, either winding (rectangle and ellipse build common ones). Shapes may cross the cell edge and are periodised; they must not overlap each other or their images.
  • Orders. Order (m, n) has in-plane wavevector (kx₀ + m·λ/Λx, ky₀ + n·λ/Λy), resolved into its own p and s. max_order=(Mx, My) keeps (2Mx + 1)(2My + 1) harmonics; cost grows as their cube, so a few hundred is a practical ceiling on a CPU.
  • Batching. Tensors, thicknesses and vertices may carry batch dimensions, and the solve can be jax.jit-compiled (max_order, factorization static).
  • Four-port S-matrix. crossed_grating_smatrix gives the zeroth-order PlanarSMatrix for SAX circuits (Scattering Matrices and SAX), on bcm.stack_smatrix's normalisation; kx= replaces the angle, allowing evanescent ports.
  • Crystal substrates. eps_exit may be a 3×3 tensor (anisotropic, hyperbolic or absorbing). Each order's two transmitted modes, power-normalised, replace p and s.

docs.title: Lattices
docs.text:
Any Bravais lattice, given by its primitive vectors:

hexagonal = rcwa2d.Lattice.hexagonal(0.6)                 # triangular, a1 along x
oblique = rcwa2d.Lattice.oblique(0.7, 0.6, jnp.radians(75.0))
custom = rcwa2d.Lattice((0.6, 0.0), (0.3, 0.52))

holes = rcwa2d.PatternedLayer(0.25, 12.25 * eye,
                              (rcwa2d.Shape(rcwa2d.ellipse((0.0, 0.0), (0.18, 0.18)), eye),))
result = rcwa2d.solve_crossed_grating(
    [holes], hexagonal, wavelength_um=1.0, incidence_rad=0.3, eps_incident=1.0,
    eps_exit=2.1, max_order=(6, 6), truncation="circular",
)

truncation="circular" keeps every G = m·b₁ + n·b₂ with |G| ≤ max(M₁, M₂)·g_min: it respects the lattice's symmetry (hexagonal included) and does not depend on the primitive vectors chosen, but needs a concrete lattice. To optimise a lattice constant, use the default "parallelogram" (|m| ≤ M₁, |n| ≤ M₂).

docs.title: Fourier factorisation
docs.text: factorization="normal" (default) is the normal-vector method generalised to full tensors: Li's anisotropic rule in a local frame normal to the pattern's edges, symmetrised so that lossless cells conserve energy at every truncation (details in the API reference). "laurent" uses Toeplitz matrices of ε and converges more slowly where E's normal component jumps.

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text:
The normal-vector rule converges faster than Laurent's: on a birefringent disc (Λ = 0.6 µm, h = 0.25 µm, λ = 1 µm), R_pp is 0.00533 / 0.00539 at 121 / 529 harmonics, against FMMAX's 0.00543 at 1605, and Laurent's 0.00305 / 0.00415. On the tilted-axis LiNbO₃ nanofins of arXiv:2608.06185, which FMMAX cannot represent, T_xx at 550 nm is 0.9520 at 289 harmonics, against the paper's 0.9496 (BCM) and 0.9483 (FEM). Metal and hyperbolic inclusions converge slowly under any rule: check a design at two truncations.

Tests: tests/test_rcwa2d.py.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The incident half-space must be isotropic and lossless.
  • Plane-wave results for an infinitely periodic structure.

docs.title: Differentiable Solver (JAX)
docs.text: hyperbolic_optics.bcm solves the same planar problem as Structure, written in JAX so that jax.grad gives exact derivatives of any result with respect to layer thicknesses, tensor components (including loss), crystal orientations, the angle of incidence and the wavelength. Use it for gradient-based design. The payload API is unchanged and remains the reference.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
JAX is an optional dependency:

pip install "hyperbolic-optics[jax]"
# or, in a checkout
uv sync --extra jax

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
Enable 64-bit JAX first (the setting is global, so the package leaves it to you):

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

Without it the solver runs in complex64 and warns.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The solver is a function of arrays, not payloads. Tensors are given in the lab frame, with the plane of incidence x-z:

import jax.numpy as jnp
from hyperbolic_optics import bcm

# LiNbO3 film, extraordinary axis in-plane at 45°, on glass
crystal = jnp.diag(jnp.array([5.06, 5.46, 5.46], dtype=complex))
film = bcm.rotate_tensor(crystal, bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, 0.0, jnp.radians(45.0)))

result = bcm.solve_stack(
    eps=film[None],                      # [L, 3, 3], incident side first
    thickness_um=jnp.array([3.6]),       # [L]
    wavelength_um=jnp.linspace(0.6, 0.7, 41),
    incidence_rad=0.0,
    eps_incident=1.0,
    eps_exit=1.52**2,
)
result.T[..., 1, 0]  # p in, s out: transmitted power

result has r, t (complex) and R, T (power), each [..., out, in] with index 0 = p and 1 = s. The complex coefficients use the same sign convention as Structure, so result.r[..., 0, 0] is r_pp and result.r[..., 1, 0] is r_ps (p in, s out). Every argument broadcasts over leading batch dimensions, and mu= takes permeability tensors in the same layout.

For a frequency in cm⁻¹, pass wavelength_um = 1e4 / frequency. rotation_matrix(x, y, z) follows the payload's rotationX/rotationY/ rotationZ convention, so a tensor rotated with it matches the one a Crystal Layer would use.

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
def objective(thickness):
    res = bcm.solve_stack(film[None], thickness[None], 0.65, 0.0, 1.0, 1.52**2)
    return res.T[1, 0]

jax.grad(objective)(jnp.asarray(3.6))

Wrap repeated calls in jax.jit(..., static_argnames="doublings"). examples/optimize_polarization_converter.py optimises a film's thickness and axis angle with Adam, then re-checks the result with Structure.

docs.title: Fields and layer-resolved absorption
docs.text:
lossy = film + 0.05j * jnp.eye(3)
fields = bcm.stack_fields(lossy[None], jnp.array([3.6]), 0.65, 0.3, 1.0, 1.52**2,
                          samples_per_layer=100)
fields.absorption      # [..., L, 2]: absorbed fraction per layer, for p and s in
fields.R, fields.T     # [..., 2]
fields.interface_flux  # [..., L + 1, 2]: S_z at each interface over the incident flux
fields.z_um, fields.fields   # depths, and (Ex, Ey, Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz) there, per polarization

Fields at each plane come from the scattering matrices above and below it, never from transfer matrices, so thick, absorbing and evanescent layers stay finite. Samples sit at fixed fractions of each layer, so gradients include the thicknesses. Each layer's absorption is checked against the loss density integrated over its depth (tests/test_stack_fields.py).

docs.title: Stacks on bulk crystals
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics import dispersion

calcite = bcm.rotate_tensor(dispersion.permittivity("Calcite", 1470.0),
                            bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, jnp.radians(65.0), jnp.radians(30.0)))
result = bcm.solve_stack_on_crystal(
    eps=jnp.eye(3, dtype=complex)[None], thickness_um=jnp.array([1.0]),   # an air gap
    wavelength_um=1e4 / 1470.0, incidence_rad=0.6, eps_incident=5.5, eps_substrate=calcite,
)
result.r, result.R, result.T      # T: power carried into the crystal, per input

The NumPy engine's Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer, differentiable: any crystal in any orientation, lossy, lossless or hyperbolic. The outgoing waves come from a matrix sign function rather than eigenvectors, so degenerate modes (an optic axis along z at normal incidence) have finite gradients.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Each layer's scattering matrix is built without eigendecomposition. The field equation dF/dz = iΔF is integrated over a slice k₀d / 2ᴺ thin by a fourth-order Taylor series, and the slice is doubled N times (default 20) by star products. Only matrix products and linear solves are used, so there are no eigenvector derivatives to diverge where modes are degenerate. This is the bisection-doubling scheme of the boundary-value cascade method of Yang, Song & Cai (arXiv:2608.06185).

Unlike the paper's E/H form, which is singular when a lossless layer is an odd number of quarter-waves thick, the doubling works on power-normalised wave amplitudes in a reference medium with kz = √(1 + kx²), so no step meets a singular inverse. The start-up series is derived independently of the paper's supplement: a related implementation, not a reproduction.

Tests: tests/test_bcm.py (closed forms, the NumPy engine to ~1e-14, gradients, energy) and tests/test_crystal_substrates.py.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• solve_stack and stack_smatrix need isotropic, lossless half-spaces; use solve_stack_on_crystal for a crystal substrate.
  • For wavelength derivatives that include the material's dispersion, take the tensor from hyperbolic_optics.dispersion (the built-in materials in JAX), not from the NumPy material classes, which carry no gradient.
  • Exact grazing cutoff in the exit medium (kx equal to its index) is singular, as in any plane-wave basis.

docs.title: gdsfactory Integration
docs.text:
hyperbolic_optics.integrations.gdsfactory (hog) reads PDK layer stacks and gdsfactory layouts into the solvers, with crystal cuts stated, draws metasurfaces cell by cell, and exports SAX models.

pip install "hyperbolic-optics[gdsfactory]"     # or: uv sync --extra gdsfactory

It needs gdsfactory >=9.51,<10 and JAX >=0.9.2,<0.12; SAX is optional (see SAX).

gdsfactory needs an active PDK before it draws anything:

import gdsfactory as gf
import jax
import numpy as np

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
gf.gpdk.PDK.activate()     # or your own PDK

from hyperbolic_optics.integrations import gdsfactory as hog

docs.title: Stacks from a PDK
docs.text:
from gdsfactory.technology import LayerLevel, LayerStack, LogicalLayer

# x-cut thin-film LiNbO3 on insulator; ribs on layer (2, 0) etched 0.3 µm
wafer = LogicalLayer(layer=gf.get_layer("WAFER"))
tfln = LayerStack(layers={
    "substrate": LayerLevel(layer=wafer, zmin=-3.0, thickness=1.0, material="si", mesh_order=100),
    "box": LayerLevel(layer=wafer, zmin=-2.0, thickness=2.0, material="sio2", mesh_order=9),
    "ln_slab": LayerLevel(layer=wafer, zmin=0.0, thickness=0.3, material="ln", mesh_order=2),
    "ln_rib": LayerLevel(layer=LogicalLayer(layer=(2, 0)), zmin=0.3, thickness=0.3,
                         material="ln", mesh_order=2),
})
materials = {"ln": hog.Oriented("LiNbO3", hog.x_cut(0.0))}   # the cut: yours to state

ribs = hog.line_grating(period_um=1.2, fill=0.5, n_periods=12, layer=(2, 0))
grating, stack, diffraction = hog.simulate_grating(
    ribs, (2, 0), tfln, wavelengths_um=[1.55], angles_deg=[30.0], materials=materials,
)
slab, planar = hog.simulate_stack(
    ribs, tfln, point_um=(0.9, 10.0), wavelengths_um=[1.55],
    angles_deg=[0.0, 30.0, 60.0], azimuths_deg=[0.0, 45.0], materials=materials,
)
planar.mueller().shape      # (1, 3, 2, 4, 4): [wavelength, angle, azimuth, 4, 4]
  • The column at a point. Levels on WAFER are everywhere; others where their layer has shapes, derived layers included. Where levels overlap, the lowest mesh_order wins. The lowest level is the exit half-space, and ambient (air) the incident one. Gaps and mesh-order ties between materials are refused. For 2D-periodic cells the exit may be a crystal or absorbing wafer, whose two transmitted modes replace p and s.
  • Gratings and 2D patterns. grating_stack and crossed_grating_stack compare the column inside the shapes with the column around them. Where they differ the layer is patterned, so etch depth and groove fill come from the PDK.
  • Materials. materials maps the PDK's names onto DEFAULT_MATERIALS (si, sio2, sin, air). A value is a built-in name ("LiNbO3", "TiO2", "hBN", "MoO3", …, with dispersion), a number or 3×3 tensor, a callable λ → ε, or Oriented(material, rotation_deg).
  • Orientation. An anisotropic PDK material has no default, because the PDK can't know the wafer cut. Use x_cut(azimuth_deg), z_cut(), or any payload-style rotation.
  • Results. PlanarResponse over [wavelength, angle, azimuth] and GratingResponse / CrossedGratingResponse over [wavelength, angle, order] carry r, t, R and T ([..., out, in], 0 = p, 1 = s), plus mueller() and ellipsometry(). solver="numpy" runs the eigenmode engine instead of JAX; the two agree to rounding.

examples/tfln_gdsfactory.py runs this on Luxtelligence's LNOI400 PDK (uv run --with lnoi400 …). It reads the rib waveguide and a partially etched grating whose grooves are filled with SiO₂.

docs.title: Line gratings and periodic arrays
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics import rcwa, rcwa2d

component = hog.line_grating(period_um=2.65, fill=0.72, n_periods=30, layer=(1, 0))
component.write_gds("absorber.gds")
grating = hog.extract_line_grating(gf.import_gds("absorber.gds"), layer=(1, 0))
stack = [hog.StackLayer(0.148, "hBN", background=1.0), hog.StackLayer(1.48, 1.85)]
result = rcwa.solve_grating(hog.grating_layers(grating, stack, 1e4 / 1500), grating.period_um,
                            1e4 / 1500, 0.0, 1.0, 11.7, 40)

disc = tuple(map(tuple, rcwa2d.ellipse((0.3, 0.25), (0.12, 0.08), 48).tolist()))
array = hog.periodic_array(period_um=(0.6, 0.5), polygons=(disc,), n_cells=(20, 20),
                           layer=(2, 0))
cell, stack, response = hog.simulate_crossed_grating(
    array, (2, 0), tfln, wavelengths_um=[1.55], angles_deg=[0.0, 10.0],
    max_order=(5, 5), materials=materials,
)
response.R[0, 0, response.order(0, 0)]      # [out, in] of the zeroth order
  • The PCells snap every vertex and lattice vector to the layout grid, so the GDS is exactly periodic.
  • extract_line_grating and extract_unit_cell read the pattern back from any layout. extract_unit_cell infers the lattice: rectangular, hexagonal or oblique, dimers included. Anything that is not exactly periodic is refused, never approximated.
  • grating_layers and crossed_grating_layers take JAX values throughout (fill, polygons, thicknesses, wavelength), so designs can be optimised and then drawn.

examples/moo3_metasurface_gdsfactory.py optimises α-MoO₃ pillars and the crystal's in-plane angle for cross-polarized reflection, then draws, reads back and re-simulates the design.

docs.title: Metasurfaces with different cells at every site
docs.text:
A cell is a VerticalStack whose layers carry their own polygons, about the cell's centre; each layer has its own material, thickness, shapes and orientation. cell_from_pdk reads one from a centred layout through the PDK: gaps become ambient spacers, shapes crossing the cell's edge wrap around, the lowest interval must be uniform, and each other interval may hold at most two materials.

mask = gf.Component()
mask.add_polygon([(-0.12, -0.05), (0.12, -0.05), (0.12, 0.05), (-0.12, 0.05)], layer=(2, 0))
pdk_cell = hog.cell_from_pdk(mask, tfln, ((0.4, 0.0), (0.0, 0.4)), materials=materials)

sidewall_slices=N models tapered levels by N slices, from the PDK's sidewall_angle, width_to_z and scalar bias; otherwise walls are vertical and a warning names the ignored process geometry.

from hyperbolic_optics import metasurfaces as ms

ln = hog.Oriented("LiNbO3", hog.x_cut(0.0))
fin = (np.array([[-0.125, -0.05], [0.125, -0.05], [0.125, 0.05], [-0.125, 0.05]]),)


def cell(twist_deg, n_twisted):
    """n LiNbO3 films, each turned twist_deg further, under a TiO2 fin."""
    films = tuple(hog.StackLayer(0.1, ln, rotation_deg=(0, 0, k * twist_deg))
                  for k in range(n_twisted))
    top = hog.StackLayer(0.3, 2.4**2, background=1.0, polygons=fin, name="fin")
    return hog.VerticalStack(films + (top,), incident=1.0, exit=1.45**2)


lattice = ((0.4, 0.0), (0.0, 0.4))
sites = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.4, 0.0], [0.8, 0.0]])
cells = [cell(0, 1), cell(30, 2), cell(45, 3)]
layout = hog.metasurface_component(sites, cells, [(10, 0), (11, 0), (12, 0), (13, 0)],
                                   lattice, rotations_rad=[0.0, 0.3, 0.6])
layout.write_gds("metasurface.gds")
sites_back, cells_back, _ = hog.read_metasurface(gf.import_gds("metasurface.gds"))

model = hog.cell_sax_model(cells_back[0], lattice, max_order=(3, 3))   # SAX: wl, kx, azimuth
model(wl=0.633)["top@p", "bottom@s"]
  • Layout. Each distinct cell is drawn once, level k on layers[k], with its materials in the cell's info; every site is a reference, turned if asked (the lattice never turns). Crystals turn with the reference unless rotate_materials=False (a mask on a wafer with fixed axes; hog.turned takes the same flag). Shapes that, turned, overlap each other or their periodic images are refused; off-grid vertices warn.
  • Reading back. read_metasurface gives each site's cell, geometry from the drawn polygons and materials from info (callables by name, through materials=). Nested layouts, arrays, mirrors and magnification are refused.
  • From a PDK. Cells may instead be gf.Components drawn on PDK layers; read_metasurface(layout, materials, layer_stack=…) reads each site through cell_from_pdk, turned as placed, crystals on the wafer's axes.
  • Solving. hog.cell_layers(cell, λ) gives a cell's rcwa2d layers; ms.cell_library solves a batch in one compiled, differentiable call (zero-thickness layers pad cells to a common layer count). ms.lens_phase, ms.choose_cells, ms.sample_grid and ms.focus design a lens by local periodicity: each cell as in an infinite array of itself. Six x-cut LiNbO₃ fins turned by kπ/6 on a fixed wafer, solved as one supercell, put 0.40 of the power into the deflected order where their library entries predict 0.37.

examples/metalens_gdsfactory.py turns 300 × 110 × 600 nm TiO₂ fins in a fixed 325 nm lattice at 660 nm. Converged (--max-order 16), a fin converts 0.86 at 0° but about 0.675 near 45°, and the lens designed from that library focuses 0.59 of the power within 1.5 FWHM, against 0.70 for ideal rotators.

docs.title: SAX models and S-parameters
docs.text:
• hog.stack_sax_model(stack) and hog.cell_sax_model(cell, lattice) give SAX models of a stack and of a cell's zeroth order (see SAX).
  • hog.write_sparameters_stack and hog.write_sparameters_cell cache them gplugins-style as .npz, keyed on the evaluated materials and thicknesses; hog.model_from_npz reads one back with the polarization modes kept.
strip = gf.components.straight(length=10, width=0.5)
sp = hog.write_sparameters_stack(strip, gf.get_active_pdk().layer_stack, (5.0, 0.0),
                                 np.linspace(1.5, 1.6, 3), angle_deg=20.0, dirpath="sparameters")
hog.model_from_npz(sp)(wl=1.55)[("top@p", "bottom@s")]

cell_sp = hog.write_sparameters_cell(cells_back[0], lattice, [0.63, 0.64],
                                    max_order=(1, 1), dirpath="sparameters")
hog.model_from_npz(cell_sp)(wl=0.633)[("top@p", "bottom@s")]

For a PDK cell, pass hog.cell_from_pdk(component, layer_stack, lattice, materials) to write_sparameters_cell.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Capability Status PDK layers, crystal cuts, anisotropic periodic-cell gradients Supported Linear sidewalls and scalar bias Sliced approximation; refinement required Cached four-port plane-wave models Supported; closed model only below diffraction thresholds Finite metasurface Local periodicity and scalar propagation Guided waveguide ports or a waveguide/free-space bridge Not provided Independent full-wave comparison One rotated biaxial periodic cell; see benchmarks/validation/README.md in the repository
  • A line grating or periodic_array has one etch shared by every patterned layer; metasurface cells give each layer its own polygons.
  • Gradients with respect to edge positions can ripple on hyperbolic ridges; see Gratings.

docs.title: Gratings (RCWA)
docs.text:
hyperbolic_optics.rcwa computes diffraction by structures that are periodic in x, uniform in y and layered in z. Any segment of any layer can have a full 3×3 permittivity and permeability, including the xz and yz components of a tilted crystal axis, and incidence can be conical. It is written in JAX like the differentiable planar solver and uses the same eigendecomposition-free layer engine, so jax.grad works with respect to:

  • geometry: fill factor, ridge position, thickness, period
  • materials and their orientation
  • wavelength and incidence

It needs the optional JAX dependency and 64-bit JAX, as the planar solver does.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
import jax.numpy as jnp
from hyperbolic_optics import bcm, rcwa

eye = jnp.eye(3, dtype=complex)
# LiNbO3 ridges with the optic axis tilted 45° out of plane, in air
crystal = jnp.diag(jnp.array([5.06, 5.46, 5.46], dtype=complex))
ridge = bcm.rotate_tensor(crystal, bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, jnp.radians(45.0), 0.0))

layers = [
    rcwa.lamellar_layer(ridge, eye, fill=0.4, thickness_um=0.35),
    rcwa.uniform_layer(2.1 * eye, 0.1),         # an unpatterned film below it
]
result = rcwa.solve_grating(
    layers,
    period_um=0.9,
    wavelength_um=1.0,
    incidence_rad=jnp.radians(20.0),
    eps_incident=1.0,
    eps_exit=1.45**2,
    max_order=15,                               # keeps orders −15 … 15
)
result.orders           # [-15 … 15]
result.T[..., 1, 0]     # per order: p in, s out, as a diffraction efficiency

r and t are complex amplitudes, and R and T are efficiencies. Each is indexed [..., order, out, in] with 0 = p and 1 = s, and each order is resolved into its own p and s relative to its plane of diffraction. Only the zeroth order is incident. Evanescent orders have zero efficiency.

Build layers with:

  • uniform_layer(eps, thickness) — unpatterned
  • lamellar_layer(eps_ridge, eps_groove, fill, thickness, offset=0.0) — a ridge and a groove per period
  • sampled_layer(eps_samples, thickness) — any profile, sampled at equal widths
  • GratingLayer(thickness, boundaries, eps) — segments with arbitrary edges

Edges enter through exact Fourier coefficients, so derivatives with respect to fill and offset are exact rather than pixelated. A profile that also varies in z, such as a slanted or twisted grating, is a stack of thin layers.

docs.title: What materials it handles
docs.text:
Every segment takes a full 3×3 ε and μ: isotropic dielectrics and metals, in-plane anisotropic and hyperbolic crystals (LiNbO₃, α-MoO₃), full tensors with xz and yz terms (tilted hBN) and non-symmetric, gyrotropic tensors. The isotropic and in-plane cases agree with FMMAX to 4e-7–1e-4 (the comparison script is in git history before 98a1f20); full tensors, which FMMAX cannot represent, agree with an eigenmode solution to 1e-10 and, unpatterned, with the NumPy engine to 1e-14.

  • ε_xx, ε_zz, μ_xx and μ_zz must be nonzero: Li's rule divides by them. Any loss keeps a near-zero value finite.
  • Incident and exit half-spaces must be isotropic and lossless.

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text:
Truncation is the main error: raise max_order until the quantity you need stops changing. With Li's factorisation, the change to the 161-order result is roughly:

grating 41 orders 81 orders silicon ridge in air 1e-4 3e-5 gold ridge, TM 1e-2 2e-3 LiNbO₃, axis in the plane 5e-5 9e-6 hyperbolic MoO₃, axis in the plane 7e-4 2e-4 hyperbolic hBN, axis tilted (full tensor) 2e-2 6e-3

Hyperbolic ridges carry very high-k waves, so plan on 81 orders or more. Doublings grow with max_order automatically (rcwa.default_doublings). Lossless gratings conserve energy to 1e-13 (dielectric, 41 orders) down to 3e-8 (hyperbolic, 161 orders), far below the truncation error.

docs.title: Gradients with respect to geometry on hyperbolic ridges
docs.text:
On some hyperbolic ridges (tilted-axis hBN) the truncated model ripples with the edge positions; the ripple's amplitude falls with max_order but its frequency rises, so the gradient's ripple persists. Compare gradients at two truncations; if they ripple, set edge_width (a fraction of the period: coefficient m is multiplied by sinc(m·edge_width)) and re-simulate the hard-edged layout to measure the shift.

Tests: tests/test_rcwa.py.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Periodic in one direction only; for 2D see Crossed Gratings (2D RCWA).
  • Plane-wave results for an infinitely periodic structure.

docs.title: Jones Calculus
docs.text:
Mueller matrices work at the intensity level: they handle depolarization but discard absolute phase. Jones is the amplitude-level counterpart — 2×2 complex matrices and 2-component vectors that preserve phase, which is what you want for fully-polarized coherent light.

A structure's reflection coefficients already are a Jones matrix:

J = [[r_pp, r_ps],
     [r_sp, r_ss]]     rows = output p/s, columns = input p/s

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Every snippet on this page follows on from:

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {"type": "Incident"},
    "Layers": [
        {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
        {
            "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
            "material": "Calcite",
            "rotationY": 90,
        },
    ],
}

from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure
from hyperbolic_optics.jones import Jones

structure = Structure()
structure.execute(payload)

jones = Jones(structure)
jones.set_incident_polarization("linear", angle=0)    # p-polarized
jones.add_optical_component("sample")
jones.add_optical_component("linear_polarizer", 90)   # crossed analyzer
extinction = jones.get_intensity()

Ideal components (linear_polarizer, quarter_wave_plate, half_wave_plate, rotator) are angle-independent and broadcast over any scenario sweep.

docs.title: Eigenpolarizations and exceptional points
docs.text:
The eigenvectors of J are the states that reflect without polarization conversion — J·v = λ·v, so the state comes back scaled by a complex λ but otherwise unchanged.

data = jones.eigenpolarizations()
data["eigenvalues"]          # [..., 2]
data["eigenpolarizations"]   # [..., 2, 2], columns are the eigenvectors
data["discriminant"]         # -> 0 at an exceptional point
data["eigenvector_overlap"]  # -> 1 at an exceptional point

Index 0 is the more p-like eigenvector, index 1 the more s-like. That labelling matters: np.linalg.eig returns them in no particular order, so without it the two swap arbitrarily across a sweep and any per-channel map inherits seams that are not physical. Ordering by |λ| — the obvious alternative — is much worse, seaming along every |λ₀| = |λ₁| contour.

A reflection Jones matrix from a lossy anisotropic sample is generally non-normal: its eigenvectors are not orthogonal and can coalesce at an exceptional point, where the matrix stops being diagonalizable.

found = jones.find_exceptional_points()
found["ep_index"]       # strongest candidate on the grid
found["near_ep"]        # boolean mask on eigenvector overlap
found["defectiveness"]  # scale-free, 0 where the eigenvectors truly coalesce

No labelling is globally continuous near an EP

Encircling an exceptional point exchanges the two eigenvalue sheets, so every labelling scheme owns at least one branch cut per EP. Ordering by polarization character puts its cuts on the EP chains — where a discontinuity is physically correct — and nowhere else.

docs.title: Ellipsometry
docs.text: jones.ellipsometric_parameters()    # psi and delta

docs.title: Composing elements
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics.jones import compose_jones

analyzer = jones.linear_polarizer(90)
total = compose_jones(structure, analyzer)   # beam order

Two Structure elements must share the same kx and frequency grids — the in-plane wavevector is conserved, so composing samples evaluated at different angles is not a meaningful product, and the guard rejects it.

docs.title: Bridging to Mueller
docs.text:
jones.to_mueller()

Reuses the same Jones-to-Mueller transform Mueller does, so the two formalisms stay consistent — including the handedness convention for circular polarization.

{"type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer", "material": "SiC", "rotationY": 0}
{"type": "Crystal Layer", "material": "AlN", "thickness": 1.0, "rotationY": 0}

docs.text:

    "type": "Crystal Layer",
    "material": "MoO3",
    "thickness": 1.2,
    "rotationY": 0,
    "rotationZ": 0  # azimuthal rotation exposes the in-plane anisotropy
}

docs.text:
Lossless Sellmeier fits for the transparency windows, where photonic chips work:

name crystal valid (µm) source LiNbO3 congruent lithium niobate, negative uniaxial 0.4–5.0 Zelmon et al., JOSA B 14, 3319 (1997) TiO2 rutile, positive uniaxial 0.43–1.53 DeVore, JOSA 41, 416 (1951) QuartzSellmeier α-quartz 0.198–2.05 Ghosh, Opt. Commun. 163, 95 (1999) CalciteSellmeier calcite 0.204–2.172 Ghosh (1999) SapphireSellmeier α-Al₂O₃ 0.2–5.5 Malitson & Dodge, JOSA 62, 1405 (1972) SiO2 fused silica, isotropic 0.21–6.7 Malitson, JOSA 55, 1205 (1965) Si3N4 LPCVD silicon nitride, isotropic 0.31–5.5 Luke et al., Opt. Lett. 40, 4823 (2015) Si crystalline silicon, isotropic 1.36–11 Salzberg & Villa, JOSA 47, 244 (1957)
