docs.title: Guided Modes, Pockels Effect and Beam Shifts
Guided modes of anisotropic stacks
docs.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

from hyperbolic_optics import bcm, dispersion, modes

# x-cut LiNbO3, 0.6 µm, optic axis in the plane at 45° to the propagation direction
rotation = bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, np.radians(90.0), np.radians(45.0))
eps = bcm.rotate_tensor(dispersion.at_wavelength("LiNbO3", 1.55), rotation)[None]
thickness_um = jnp.array([0.6])
found = modes.slab_modes(eps, thickness_um, wavelength_um=1.55, eps_top=1.0,
                         eps_bottom=1.444**2)
z_um, fields = modes.slab_mode_fields(eps, thickness_um, 1.55, 1.0, 1.444**2,
                                      found[0].effective_index)
  • Any 3 × 3 ε and μ in any layer. In a rotated crystal the modes are hybrid, neither TE nor TM. Lossy layers give a complex n_eff.
  • Modes propagate along x; rotate the tensors to change direction.
  • Indefinite tensors need an explicit index_range above both cladding indices. Unresolved contours raise rather than return a partial list, and modes just above cutoff are found (the default search starts 1e-6 above it).
  • slab_mode_fields returns E and H through the stack and into the claddings, normalised to unit power along x.

Tests: tests/test_modes.py (analytic slab modes, absorbed power, prism coupling in the NumPy engine).

docs.title: The Pockels effect
docs.text:
dispersion.pockels_tensor gives ε under an applied field, for a crystal in any orientation and a field in any direction. It is differentiable, so a voltage is a design parameter for every solver here. A mode's index shift is the change in its root:

ln = dispersion.at_wavelength("LiNbO3", 1.55)
x_cut = bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, np.radians(90.0), np.radians(90.0))   # axis along y


def index(volts_per_um):
    field = jnp.array([0.0, volts_per_um, 0.0])
    film = dispersion.pockels_tensor(ln, dispersion.LITHIUM_NIOBATE, field, x_cut)[None]
    return modes.slab_modes(film, thickness_um, 1.55, 1.0, 1.444**2)[0].effective_index


dn_per_v_per_um = (index(0.5) - index(-0.5)).real

LITHIUM_NIOBATE holds the unclamped coefficients measured at 633 nm (Weis & Gaylord 1985). trigonal_3m(r13, r22, r33, r51) builds a tensor from other data, and any 3 × 3 × 3 tensor is accepted.

docs.title: Beam shifts
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics import beams

x, y, field = beams.reflected_beam(eps, thickness_um, 1.55, np.radians(40.0), 1.5**2, 1.0,
                                   waist_um=10.0, polarization=np.array([1, 1j]) / np.sqrt(2))
dx, dy = beams.beam_shift(x, y, field)      # Goos–Hänchen and Imbert–Fedorov shifts, µm

A Gaussian beam is a superposition of plane waves, each passing through the stack with its own S-matrix. At total internal reflection the Goos–Hänchen shift matches Artmann's −dφ/dq_x. The Imbert–Fedorov shift flips sign with the helicity (tests/test_beams.py).

docs.title: Mueller Matrices
docs.text: Mueller matrices describe how light's polarization state changes upon reflection from a surface.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Every snippet on this page follows on from:

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {"type": "Incident"},
    "Layers": [
        {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
        {
            "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
            "material": "Calcite",
            "rotationY": 90,
        },
    ],
}

from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure
from hyperbolic_optics.mueller import Mueller

# Create structure
structure = Structure()
structure.execute(payload)

# Create Mueller analyzer
mueller = Mueller(structure)

# Each block below starts a fresh Mueller; a component may be added once.
# Set incident polarization
mueller.set_incident_polarization('linear', angle=45)

# Add the sample
mueller.add_optical_component('anisotropic_sample')

# Calculate results
params = mueller.get_all_parameters()

docs.title: Linear Polarization
docs.text:
# p-polarized (0°)
mueller.set_incident_polarization('linear', angle=0)

# s-polarized (90°)
mueller.set_incident_polarization('linear', angle=90)

# 45° linear
mueller.set_incident_polarization('linear', angle=45)

docs.title: Circular Polarization
docs.text:
# Right-handed circular
mueller.set_incident_polarization('circular', handedness='right')

# Left-handed circular
mueller.set_incident_polarization('circular', handedness='left')

docs.title: Elliptical Polarization
docs.text:
# Elliptical with azimuth 30° and ellipticity 20°
mueller.set_incident_polarization('elliptical', alpha=30, ellipticity=20)

docs.title: Anisotropic Sample
docs.text:
The main sample being analyzed:

mueller = Mueller(structure)   # a component may only be added once
mueller.add_optical_component('anisotropic_sample')

docs.title: Linear Polarizer
docs.text:
# Horizontal polarizer (0°)
mueller.add_optical_component('linear_polarizer', 0)

# Vertical polarizer (90°)
mueller.add_optical_component('linear_polarizer', 90)

# 45° polarizer
mueller.add_optical_component('linear_polarizer', 45)

docs.title: Quarter-Wave Plate
docs.text:
# QWP with fast axis at 45°
mueller.add_optical_component('quarter_wave_plate', 45)

docs.title: Half-Wave Plate
docs.text:
# HWP with fast axis at 22.5°
mueller.add_optical_component('half_wave_plate', 22.5)

docs.title: Multiple Components
docs.text:
Place components in series:

# Polarizer → Sample → Analyzer
mueller = Mueller(structure)
mueller.set_incident_polarization('linear', angle=0)
mueller.add_optical_component('linear_polarizer', 0)  # Input polarizer
mueller.add_optical_component('anisotropic_sample')    # Sample
mueller.add_optical_component('linear_polarizer', 90)  # Analyzer (crossed)

reflectivity = mueller.get_reflectivity()

docs.title: Stokes Parameters
docs.text:
The Stokes parameters describe the polarization state:

  • S0: Total intensity (reflectance)
  • S1: Horizontal vs vertical linear polarization
  • S2: +45° vs -45° linear polarization
  • S3: Right vs left circular polarization
stokes = mueller.get_stokes_parameters()

print(f"Total intensity: {stokes['S0']}")
print(f"Linear H/V: {stokes['S1']}")
print(f"Linear ±45°: {stokes['S2']}")
print(f"Circular R/L: {stokes['S3']}")

docs.title: Degree of Polarization (DOP)
docs.text:
dop = mueller.get_degree_of_polarisation()
# DOP = 0: unpolarized
# DOP = 1: fully polarized

docs.title: Ellipticity
docs.text:
ellipticity = mueller.get_ellipticity()
# Ellipticity angle in radians
# 0: linear
# ±π/4: circular

docs.title: Azimuth
docs.text:
azimuth = mueller.get_azimuth()
# Orientation of polarization ellipse major axis

docs.title: All Parameters at Once
docs.text:
params = mueller.get_all_parameters()

# Contains: S0, S1, S2, S3, DOP, Ellipticity, Azimuth
for key, value in params.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure
from hyperbolic_optics.mueller import Mueller

# Define structure
payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Incident"
    },
    "Layers": [
        {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
        {"type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer", "thickness": 0.1},
        {
            "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
            "material": "Quartz",
            "rotationX": 0,
            "rotationY": 70,
            "rotationZ": 0
        }
    ]
}

# Run simulation
structure = Structure()
structure.execute(payload)

# Mueller analysis
mueller = Mueller(structure)

# Try different incident polarizations
for angle in [0, 45, 90]:
    mueller.set_incident_polarization('linear', angle=angle)
    mueller.add_optical_component('anisotropic_sample')

    params = mueller.get_all_parameters()
    print(f"\nIncident angle: {angle}°")
    print(f"Average reflectance: {params['S0'].mean():.4f}")
    print(f"Average DOP: {params['DOP'].mean():.4f}")

    mueller.reset()  # Reset for next calculation

docs.title: Resetting the Mueller Object
docs.text:
# Clear all settings and start fresh
mueller.reset()

This clears: - Mueller matrix - Stokes parameters - Optical components - Resets incident polarization to unpolarized

docs.title: Reflectance (S0)
docs.text: Total reflected power, sum of all polarization components.

docs.title: Degree of Polarization
docs.text:
• DOP = 1: Fully polarized (pure state)
  • 0 < DOP < 1: Partially polarized
  • DOP = 0: Unpolarized (random)

docs.title: Understanding S1, S2, S3
docs.text:
• S1 > 0: More horizontal than vertical
  • S1 < 0: More vertical than horizontal
  • S2 > 0: More +45° than -45°
  • S2 < 0: More -45° than +45°
  • S3 > 0: More right-circular
  • S3 < 0: More left-circular

docs.title: Transmission, Absorption & Backends
docs.text: Structure.execute gives you reflection coefficients. Everything else — power transmittance, where the light is absorbed, the field through the stack — comes from FieldProfile, which consumes an executed structure the same way Mueller does.

docs.title: Power quantities
docs.text:
Every snippet on this page follows on from:

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {"type": "Incident"},
    "Layers": [
        {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 50.0},
        {
            "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
            "material": "Calcite",
            "rotationY": 90,
        },
    ],
}

from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure
from hyperbolic_optics.fields import FieldProfile

structure = Structure()
structure.execute(payload)

fp = FieldProfile(structure)

fp.reflectance("p")        # R
fp.transmittance("p")      # T, the flux crossing into the exit medium
fp.layer_absorption("p")   # one entry per finite interior layer
fp.summary("p")            # all of the above at once

These are computed from the propagated field, not from a closed-form transmission formula: the tangential field [Ex, Ey, Hx, Hy] is continuous across interfaces, and the normal flux S_z = ½ Re(Ex·Hy* − Ey·Hx*) at each interface gives the power crossing it.

Any polarization works — pass "p", "s", or an explicit complex (a_s, a_p) Jones pair.

flux_bookkeeping_residual is a bookkeeping check

summary() reports flux_bookkeeping_residual = max|R + T + ΣAᵢ − 1|. This is not a physics check. The per-layer absorptances are defined as successive differences of the same interface fluxes R and T are built from, so the sum telescopes and the residual is algebraically zero however wrong the fields are — it returns machine epsilon even where R exceeds 1.

Use it to catch NaN propagation. To check the physics, test passivity: every layer absorptance and T non-negative, R at most 1.

docs.title: Choosing a backend
docs.text:
The default multiplies per-layer transfer matrices. That is fast, but for thick, lossy or strongly evanescent layers the propagation terms grow exponentially and the product loses precision — long before it overflows to NaN it returns finite, plausible, wrong numbers.

structure.execute(payload, backend="scattering")

The scattering backend cascades per-layer scattering matrices with the Redheffer star product, so only decaying exponentials ever appear. It returns the same coefficients as the transfer method where that is well-conditioned, and correct ones where it is not — a thick evanescent Otto gap gives NaN under backend="transfer" and correct total reflection under backend="scattering".

FieldProfile works under either. Under the scattering backend the interface fields are recovered from the cascade rather than by propagating the transfer matrices, so the power quantities stay correct in that regime too.

transfer (default) scattering reflection / transmission coefficients ✅ ✅ reflectance / transmittance / layer_absorption ✅ ✅ field_profile (resolved with depth) ✅ ❌ stable for thick / evanescent stacks ❌ ✅

You rarely need to choose manually. The default path detects when a coefficient's 2×2 minor has cancelled down to the rounding floor and recomputes just those points with the cascade; Structure.repaired_fraction reports how many. Pass calculate_reflectivity(stabilize=False) for the literal transfer product.

docs.title: Field profiles with depth
docs.text:
profile = fp.field_profile("p")     # needs backend="transfer"
profile["z"]                        # depth axis
profile["Ex"], profile["Hy"], ...   # six field components
profile["Sz"]                       # Poynting flux vs depth

This is batched, but a full angle × frequency sweep times a depth axis times six components is memory-heavy — it is meant for Simple or a single slice.

docs.title: Sweeping layer thickness
docs.text:
A layer's thickness may be a list, which sweeps it as a fourth axis in a single execute — the eigendecomposition does not depend on thickness, so only the propagation phase broadcasts over it:

{"type": "Crystal Layer", "material": "Calcite",
 "thickness": [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0], "rotationY": 90}

Outputs gain a trailing axis: Simple gives r_pp.shape == (4,), Incident gives (F, angle, 4). At most one layer may carry a list thickness.

Slice before plotting

The map plots draw one 2-D array, so select a slice — plot_kx_frequency(structure, R[..., 0]). They will tell you if you forget.

For a 2-D thickness × thickness grid, combine a list thickness on one layer with the ThicknessSweep helper, which re-runs the stack and stacks results along a leading index:

from hyperbolic_optics import ThicknessSweep

docs.title: Scattering Matrices and SAX
docs.text: A planar stack has four ports: light can arrive from either side, in either polarization. bcm.stack_smatrix gives the full bidirectional scattering matrix over those ports, and hyperbolic_optics.integrations.sax wraps it as SAX models, so anisotropic stacks can be composed in SAX circuits and differentiated through them.

docs.title: The S-matrix contract
docs.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
import jax.numpy as jnp
from hyperbolic_optics import bcm

ln_tensor = bcm.rotate_tensor(jnp.diag(jnp.array([5.06, 5.46, 5.46], dtype=complex)),
                              bcm.rotation_matrix(0.0, 0.7, 0.4))   # LiNbO3, axis tilted
eps = jnp.stack([ln_tensor, 2.1 * jnp.eye(3)])        # [L, 3, 3], top down
smatrix = bcm.stack_smatrix(eps, jnp.array([0.4, 0.2]), wavelength_um=0.8,
                            kx=0.479, eps_top=1.0, eps_bottom=2.25)
smatrix.s            # [4, 4], [out, in] over bcm.PORTS
smatrix.propagating  # [4], False for a port evanescent in its half-space
  • Ports. bcm.PORTS = ("top@p", "top@s", "bottom@p", "bottom@s"). top is the incident-side half-space and bottom the exit side. p and s are defined in each half-space's plane of incidence (x-z), as in solve_stack. The reference planes are the stack's two outer interfaces.
  • kx, not an angle. The in-plane wavevector n·sin θ is conserved through the stack, while the angle changes from medium to medium. Stacks connected to one another must share kx.
  • Normalization. Amplitudes are scaled by √kz of their half-space.
    • Between propagating ports, |s|² is the fraction of power transferred. A lossless stack's matrix is unitary when all four ports propagate.
    • The top-incidence block is solve_stack's r, with its R and T.
  • Evanescent channels are kept. Beyond total internal reflection a port is flagged propagating = False. It keeps the same √kz scaling, with complex kz, so matrices sharing that half-space still compose correctly: a gap below the critical angle tunnels. |s|² is not a power for such a port.
  • Reciprocity. For symmetric ε and μ, s(kx) = D · s(−kx)ᵀ · D with D = diag(−1, 1, −1, 1). Reversing a wave reverses its in-plane wavevector, and the p waves' sign convention (they share the sign of Hy) flips on reversal. Gyrotropic media break it.

bcm.cascade(upper, lower) connects upper's bottom to lower's top. That is the stack of both, with the shared half-space of zero thickness, computed without SAX.

docs.title: SAX models
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics import dispersion
from hyperbolic_optics.integrations import sax as hsax

film = hsax.planar_model(
    [(lambda wl: dispersion.at_wavelength("hBN", wl), 0.1)],  # (material, thickness_um)
    eps_top=1.0, eps_bottom=11.7,
)
film(wl=6.7, kx=0.3, azimuth=0.2)    # SDict: {("top@p", "bottom@s"): ..., ...}
  • Signature. model(wl, kx, azimuth) -> SDict, keyed (in, out) over the four ports; wl is in µm and azimuth turns every layer about the normal. Materials are numbers, 3×3 tensors or callables of the wavelength.
  • From a PDK. hog.stack_sax_model(stack) takes a stack from vertical_stack.
  • Metasurface cells. hog.cell_sax_model(cell, lattice) wraps rcwa2d.crossed_grating_smatrix, the zeroth-order S-matrix, on the same ports and normalisation (see gdsfactory). Only the zeroth order is a port, so connect a cell to other elements across a spacer thick enough for its omitted orders to decay as exp(−αd); near a diffraction threshold α → 0, so check convergence with d.
  • Connections. Connect one model's bottom to another's top and pass kx as a global setting; SAX matches the @p and @s modes.
  • Gradients. Use sax.circuit(..., backend="filipsson_gunnar") (pure JAX); the default KLU backend fails in the backward pass.
  • Not a dependency. SAX pins JAX below 0.10, so this module doesn't import it: uv run --with sax python ….
  • Plane-wave ports only. Connecting them to waveguide modes needs a mode-matching step that is not provided.

docs.title: From payloads: Structure.execute → SAX
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure

structure = Structure()
structure.execute({
    "ScenarioData": {"type": "Azimuthal", "incidentAngle": 40.0, "frequency": 1470.0,
                     "azimuthal_angle": [0.0, 30.0, 60.0]},
    "Layers": [
        {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 5.5},
        {"type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer", "thickness": 1.5, "permittivity": 1.0},
        {"type": "Crystal Layer", "material": "Calcite", "thickness": 0.6, "rotationY": 70},
        {"type": "Semi Infinite Isotropic Layer", "permittivity": 2.0},
    ],
})
sd = hsax.structure_sdict(structure)     # values [A, B, F, T] = [1, 3, 1, 1]
sd["top@p", "top@s"]                     # r_ps (p in, s out) at each azimuth

Structure.execute gives only the 8 incident-side entries, and SAX treats missing entries as zero, so structure_smatrix / structure_sdict re-solve the executed tensors in JAX for all 16 (they match the engine's r and t to 1e-11). The exit must be a Semi Infinite Isotropic Layer.

docs.title: Polarization and sweep axes
docs.text:
Polarization is the port mode, so conversion is an off-diagonal entry such as ("top@p", "top@s") and composes through a circuit. Every other variable (wavelength, kx, azimuth, thickness) is an array axis of the SDict values; pass wl and kx as global settings so every element sees the same grid. All elements share the x-z p/s basis: an azimuth turns the sample, not the plane.

examples/sax_otto_calcite.py builds prism | air gap | x-cut calcite as a SAX circuit, maps the surface-polariton dip, shows p→s conversion with the axis turned, and tunes the gap to critical coupling through the circuit:

uv run --with sax python examples/sax_otto_calcite.py

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: The package supports four different scenario types for different analysis needs.

docs.title: Simple Scenario
docs.text:
Single point calculation at a specific angle, frequency, and orientation.

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Simple",
        "incidentAngle": 45.0,      # degrees
        "azimuthal_angle": 0.0,      # degrees  
        "frequency": 1460.0          # cm^-1
    },
    "Layers": [...]
}

Output shape: Scalar values for reflection coefficients

Use case: Quick calculations, debugging, single point analysis

docs.title: Incident Scenario
docs.text:
Sweeps through incident angles at multiple frequencies.

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Incident"
    },
    "Layers": [...]
}

Output shape: [410, 360] - 410 frequency points × 360 angle points

Use case: Analyzing angle-dependent behavior, finding resonances

Plotting: Use plot_kx_frequency() for frequency vs kx plots

docs.title: Azimuthal Scenario
docs.text:
Rotates the sample azimuthally at a fixed incident angle.

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Azimuthal",
        "incidentAngle": 40.0  # degrees
    },
    "Layers": [...]
}

Output shape: [410, 360] - 410 frequency points × 360 azimuthal angles

Use case: Studying rotational symmetry, in-plane anisotropy

Plotting: Use plot_mueller_azimuthal() for frequency vs β plots

docs.title: Dispersion Scenario
docs.text:
k-space dispersion at a fixed frequency.

payload = {
    "ScenarioData": {
        "type": "Dispersion",
        "frequency": 1460.0  # cm^-1
    },
    "Layers": [...]
}

Output shape: [180, 480] - 180 incident angles × 480 azimuthal angles

Use case: Visualizing polariton dispersion, identifying wave modes

Plotting: Use plot_mueller_dispersion() for kx vs ky plots

docs.title: Choosing a Scenario
docs.text: Goal Scenario Type Quick single calculation Simple Angle-dependent analysis Incident Rotational behavior Azimuthal k-space dispersion relations Dispersion

docs.title: Frequency Ranges
docs.text:
For Incident and Azimuthal scenarios, frequency ranges are automatically determined by the material:

  • Calcite: 1300-1600 cm⁻¹ (upper) or 860-920 cm⁻¹ (lower)
  • Quartz: 410-600 cm⁻¹
  • Sapphire: 210-1000 cm⁻¹
  • Gallium Oxide: 350-800 cm⁻¹

docs.title: Example: Comparing Scenarios
docs.text:
from hyperbolic_optics.structure import Structure
from hyperbolic_optics.plots import plot_kx_frequency, plot_mueller_dispersion

# Same material, different scenarios
base_layers = [
    {"type": "Ambient Incident Layer", "permittivity": 25.0},
    {"type": "Isotropic Middle-Stack Layer", "thickness": 0.5},
    {
        "type": "Semi Infinite Anisotropic Layer",
        "material": "Calcite",
        "rotationX": 0,
        "rotationY": 70,
        "rotationZ": 0
    }
]

# Incident scenario
payload_incident = {
    "ScenarioData": {"type": "Incident"},
    "Layers": base_layers
}
structure_inc = Structure()
structure_inc.execute(payload_incident)
R_inc = abs(structure_inc.r_pp)**2

# Dispersion scenario
payload_disp = {
    "ScenarioData": {"type": "Dispersion", "frequency": 1460.0},
    "Layers": base_layers
}
structure_disp = Structure()
structure_disp.execute(payload_disp)
R_disp = abs(structure_disp.r_pp)**2

# Plot both
plot_kx_frequency(structure_inc, R_inc, save_name="incident")
plot_mueller_dispersion(structure_disp, R_disp, save_name="dispersion")
